stories.summary: Keenan Allen said while he didn't expect to get traded, landing with a contending team in the 49ers has him feeling energized.
stories.detailText: SANTA CLARA, Calif. -- Wide receiver Keenan Allen was at the Indianapolis Colts facility Tuesday morning meeting with coach Shane Steichen when he was informed that he needed to see interim general manager Ed Dodds. Unaware that his name was even involved in trade discussions, Allen soon learned that he'd been traded to the San Francisco 49ers in exchange for a 2027 sixth-round pick. From there, Allen hustled home, packed a bag and got on a plane, landing in the Bay Area a little past midnight. On Wednesday, Allen woke up, took a physical at 5:45 a.m. and began acclimating himself to his new surroundings while taking note that overnight he'd gone from the AFC South basement with the 2-7 Colts to the NFC-leading Niners. That sudden change in the trajectory of his season was enough to help him through a whirlwind first day in San Francisco. "I get a little boost in the way I feel coming into the building," Allen said. "Just being a part of the guys, it's a hell of a locker room. Obviously, these guys have accomplished so much in the past years. ... I'm running on just pure energy right now." For Allen, 34, the biggest adjustment will be learning the terminology of coach Kyle Shanahan's playbook. He said conceptually the scheme is familiar, but all the words are different. Still, when asked what he expects this week, Allen said, simply, "I expect to play." Whether Allen is able to play out the rest of the season for his new team remains to be seen. He is still amid a legal investigation stemming from an Aug. 30 arrest on suspicion of two misdemeanor offenses of drunken driven in downtown Indianapolis. In September, prosecutors filed charges against Allen for operating a vehicle with alcohol concentration equivalent to .15 blood alcohol level or more and operating a vehicle while intoxicated. According to a probable cause affidavit obtained by ESPN, Allen's blood alcohol level was .224, which triggered the first of those misdemeanor charges. Sources told ESPN's Adam Schefter in September that Allen could be subject to a minimum three-game suspension from the NFL for the arrest -- with the possibility of it being longer due to the high levels of intoxication. As of Wednesday, there's no court date set for Allen, though there's a remote "attorney conference" slated for Dec. 7 as the next step in the process. Shanahan said the Niners traded for Allen knowing that a suspension was possible and acknowledged Wednesday that it's still a potential outcome. "We're just waiting," Shanahan said. "We know the league handles that. It could go either way, so waiting for them to say ... [A suspension] is still possible." For his part, Allen said he could not comment on the situation because it is an ongoing legal matter. In the meantime, Allen is doing his best to settle in with the team he nearly joined as a free agent in the offseason. Before Allen signed with the Colts, he indicated he was in talks with the 49ers about a free agent deal. Instead, he signed with the Colts and posted 40 receptions for 351 yards and a touchdown in eight games before the trade. Upon arrival in San Francisco, Allen got plenty of questions about his relationship with fellow wideout Mike Evans . In 2020, Allen and Evans exchanged words on social media when Allen tweeted that the likes of Evans, Chris Godwin and Tyreek Hill are "not a better receiver than me." Evans responded by telling Allen to "be realistic you not on my level bro." Allen laughed about it Wednesday, explaining that it's not an issue. "We squashed it a long time ago," Allen said, laughing. "Everybody wants to bring it back up obviously, but Mike's a hell of a player. He's probably better than me at this point."

stories.title: Kamario Taylor lands $7.5 million deal to return to Mississippi State
stories.summary: One man's chaos is another man's ca-ching.
stories.detailText: {"unknownError":"There has been an error","expiredError":"This video has been expired due to copyright restrictions.","unavailableError":"This content is not yet available.","georestrictedError":"This content is not available in your location.","networkId":"169843","adManagerUrl":"https://mssl.fwmrm.net/libs/adm/6.51.0/AdManager.js","serverId":"https://29773.v.fwmrm.net/ad/g/1","profileId":"169843:nbcu_web_jwp_cs_moat_https","afid":"140315314","caid":"nbcs_nbc_pft_raiderspaid_261111","csid":"nbcsports_embed_on_domain","sfid":"","adHocGroup":"","athlete":"","businessUnit":"NBC Sports","category":"","duration":"158392","event":"","externalAdvertiserId":"nbcs_nbc_pft_raiderspaid_261111","genre":"News","guid":"nbc_pft_raiderspaid_261111","league":"NFL","network":"","platform":"PC","playlist":"","show":"ProFootballTalk","sport":"Football","subtype":"","team":"Minnesota Vikings, Las Vegas Raiders","title": "How Raiders financially benefit from Cousins trade","datePublished":"","videoPageUrl": "https://www.nbcsports.com/watch/nfl/profootballtalk/how-las-vegas-raiders-financially-benefit-from-kirk-cousins-trade","availableDate":"2026-11-11T13:40:43Z","expirationDate":"","countries":""} One man's chaos is another man's ca-ching. After years of being stuck in a system that prevented them from getting fair (or any) value for their skills, efforts, and/or sacrifices, college football players are finally getting paid. And one of them is setting a new bar. Via On3.com, Mississippi State quarterback Kamario Taylor is finalizing a $7.5 million deal to return in 2027. With incentives, it could yield as much as $9 million. With Taylor under center, the Bulldogs started 4-0. Taylor has since suffered a season-ending injury. Before the injury, Taylor was regarded as one of the favorites to win the Heisman Trophy. While the development will prompt the pearl-clutchers to try to parlay the situation into more political momentum for the Protect College Sports Act, it's a reflection of the free market at work. Which is fine for those in positions of wealth and power, when it comes to their own financial position. When someone else is reaping the benefits of capitalism in a way that complicates the lives of those who have to balance the books (and to pry cash from boosters who support the NIL funds), it becomes a problem. And so they'll do whatever they have to do to roll back the gains players have made. Because free enterprise is desirable only when the people in control practice it. When the workers start getting paid according to their worth, it becomes a crisis.

stories.title: 2027 NFL draft rankings: Jordan Reid's top 50 prospects, scouting reports
stories.summary: Jordan Reid updated his rankings for the 2027 NFL draft class with 50 players -- including seven quarterbacks and an elite wide receiver prospect.
stories.detailText: With the 2026 college football season in full swing, it's time to start stacking the top prospects in the 2027 NFL draft class, which begins on April 29 in Washington, D.C. I've been watching and evaluating these players for a couple of years in some instances, and these rankings are a compilation of my scouting (both on film and in person) and conversations I've been having with scouts and evaluators around the NFL. We're going to start these rankings with 50 players, with scouting reports on the top 25, but this list will expand as the draft gets closer and closer. And these rankings will evolve -- some players will shoot up boards, others will fall and still more will ultimately return to school for another year. But this is how I currently see things in the 2027 class. Let's get to it, starting with arguably the best wide receiver prospect of the past 15-20 years. Underclassmen are marked with an asterisk, and the top names at every position are listed at the bottom. Jump to: Rankings by position 1. Jeremiah Smith , WR, Ohio State* Height: 6-4 | Weight: 222 Stats through Nov. 7: 69 receptions for 1,200 receiving yards (17.4 yards per catch) and 14 touchdowns Smith could have All-Pro potential early in his NFL career as a true No. 1 receiver. He immediately changes the offensive outlook for the team that adds him. He is sure-handed and can glide past defenders with ease. And he's equally as capable of winning with strength at the catch point. Smith's change of direction in routes needs to become sharper, as he can take too many choppy steps when working back toward passers. But he is tough to stop when allowed to attack defenses vertically. 2. Leonard Moore , CB, Notre Dame* Height: 6-2 | Weight: 197 Stats through Nov. 7: 16 tackles, five passes defensed, 43.8% completion percentage allowed With excellent length, speed and technique, Moore is the prototypical cornerback prospect. His length and physicality allow him to excel when getting hands on receivers in press man coverage. He also has the awareness to identify and defend route concepts in zone coverage. Moore has the ball skills to match receivers, routinely tracking and attacking the ball out of the air. But he needs to improve his discipline and hand timing at the top of routes. 3. Dylan Stewart , Edge, South Carolina* Height: 6-5 | Weight: 250 Stats through Nov. 7: 12 tackles, two sacks, 4.5 tackles for loss, three forced fumbles, 20% pressure rate With a slender frame, Stewart has rare burst and closing speed as a pass rusher. That allows him to wreak havoc on twists and stunts, though the tools have yet to lead to high-end production at the college level. Stewart must also become more consistent with using his length and shedding against the run. 4. Colin Simmons , Edge, Texas* Height: 6-3 | Weight: 246 Stats through Nov. 7: 25 tackles, 10.5 sacks, 16 tackles for loss, two forced fumbles, one fumble recovery, 20.5% pressure rate Simmons is an energetic and high-effort pass rusher, with a quick first step to explode past blockers. He has a nifty combination of hesitation moves and shoulder fakes. But he still needs to develop consistent counter moves, as he can get stuck if his initial move isn't effective. Simmons is a powerful run defender, using a strong base and powerful hands to keep his frame clean when setting the edge. 5. Drew Mestemaker , QB, Oklahoma State* Height: 6-3 | Weight: 215 Stats through Nov. 7: 206-of-309 passing (66.7% completion percentage) for 2,962 passing yards, 29 touchdowns and eight interceptions; 36 carries for 177 rushing yards (4.9 yards per carry) and three touchdowns Mestemaker is my top quarterback prospect despite this being only his second season as a starter in high school and college. He has an unconventional style, holding the ball at his waistline before ripping a fiery, three-quarters release. Mestemaker has the confidence to test the tightest of windows from various platforms, but that can get the best of him and lead to turnovers. Plus, he can be oblivious to underneath defenders. Mestemaker is bit of a streaky passer, though his hot streaks feature plenty of "wow" moments. And he is capable of being a running threat. 6. Chris Cole , LB, Georgia* Height: 6-3 | Weight: 235 Stats through Nov. 7: 58 tackles, five sacks, 11 tackles for loss, three fumble recoveries, three passes defensed Cole is an easy moving, urgent defender from the second level. He has excellent lateral agility and pursuit speed to close on ball carriers in a hurry. But his ability to read and react to run concepts is still a work in progress, as his eyes can get fixated in the wrong spots. And he can be slow at recognizing concepts in zone coverage, leading to easy catches in his area. Cole is frequently used as a blitzer, which he does effectively. 7. Charlie Becker , WR, Indiana* Height: 6-4 | Weight: 208 Stats through Nov. 7: 50 receptions for 875 receiving yards (17.5 ypc) and nine touchdowns Becker is primarily used as a vertical threat, and there are few college players who can match his straight-ahead speed. But he is more than just a threat with his legs; he's similar to an NBA rebounder with the way he wins 50-50 passes. That ability comes from a combination of elite body control at the catch point and A-plus hand-eye coordination, which helps him see the ball in slow motion. Becker does need to round out his route tree, showing NFL teams that he has more branches on it than just vertical patterns. 8. Ashton Hampton , CB, Clemson* Height: 6-2 | Weight: 205 Stats through Nov. 7: 35 tackles, two interceptions for 2 yards, 12 passes defensed, 26.8% completion percentage allowed Hampton is a physically imposing cornerback who strives to humiliate receivers at the line of scrimmage by getting his hands on them. Since most receivers struggle to untangle from his coverage, he would be ideal for press man coverage schemes at the next level. Hampton is also a forceful tackler on the perimeter, with lots of knockback strength when coming into contact with ball carriers. But he does need to be more disciplined with his timing in coverage. 9. Ellis Robinson IV , CB, Georgia* Height: 6-0 | Weight: 180 Stats through Nov. 7: 19 tackles, two interceptions for 8 yards, six passes defensed, 48.1% completion percentage allowed Robinson is an ultra-athletic cornerback whose quick feet and sudden change of direction helps him stay connected in man coverage. But there are times when Robinson gives up big gains because his technique tends to be abandoned. His best reps come in zone coverage, where he has a great feel for concepts unfolding. Robinson has excellent awareness with attacking the ball in flight, and he has a linebacker-like appetite for contact in run support. 10. Will Echoles , DT, Ole Miss* Height: 6-3 | Weight: 315 Stats through Nov. 7: 22 tackles, 2.5 sacks, four tackles for loss, five passes defensed An explosive 3-technique, Echoles is one of the most versatile and well-conditioned interior defenders in the country. He has energetic hands that help him accelerate past blockers, and reliable lower body strength helps him be a malleable run defender. Echoles still needs to make major improvements in his counter moves, as he can get stuck on blockers when his power and initial moves are matched. Plus, he can get caught not being firm on contact and get moved off his spot. 11. Jordan Seaton , OT, LSU* Height: 6-5 | Weight: 307 Stats through Nov. 7: 612 snaps, 0.9% pressure rate allowed, 1.2% blown run block rate Seaton combines a good blend of awareness, quick hands and lower-body suddenness to be a high-level pass protector. He's also an easy mover in space, which allows him to excel as a puller or on screen plays. Seaton can be trusted on an island, but his biggest area of improvement must come as a run blocker. His hands and feet are inconsistent when driving on blocks to the second level. 12. Greg Johnson , C, Minnesota Height: 6-6 | Weight: 325 Stats through Nov. 7: 531 snaps, 0.3% pressure rate allowed, 0.5% blown run block rate Johnson is a hulking interior blocker whose strength helps him latch and sustain at the point of attack. He has a reliable anchor that helps him tether his feet and quickly stall pass-rush moves. In gap run schemes, Johnson has shown quickness when pulling. In zone run schemes, Johnson can be fluid enough to climb and cover up linebackers on the second level. A lot of Johnson's losses are a result of him relying solely on his upper body to generate torque and movement. His recovery athleticism is average, and he can face challenges when forced to readjust after being beaten quickly around either shoulder. 13. CJ Carr , QB, Notre Dame* Height: 6-2 | Weight: 215 Stats through Nov. 7: 177-of-262 passing (67.6%) for 2,168 passing yards and 21 touchdowns to one interception; 26 carries for 89 rushing yards (3.4 ypc) and three touchdowns Carr is a refined pocket passer whose eyes, feet and throwing motion are always in cohesion. With an easy throwing motion, he is a decisive passer who trusts his eyes to pick apart defenses. He has a great feel for the types of passes that are needed, putting enough touch or velocity on them. And he is routinely in control at the line of scrimmage with protections and when calling audibles. Carr's overall arm strength and velocity are average. And he sometimes creates chaotic negative losses trying to make a positive play instead of moving on to the next play. 14. Xavier Gilliam , DT, Tennessee* Height: 6-2 | Weight: 305 Stats through Nov. 7: 26 tackles, six sacks, 10.5 tackles for loss, two forced fumbles, one fumble recovery, two passes defensed Gilliam is an explosive, upfield interior defender who can penetrate the first level with ease. His game centers around quickness, as his first step is difficult for blockers to match. Gilliam's active hands help him win with multiple plans of attack in pass-rush situations. He is equally as strong as a run defender, anchoring his feet in the ground to withstand at the point of attack. He also can stack and dislodge blocking attempts to knock run concepts off-schedule. 15. Zereoue Williams , OT, Utah Height: 6-8 | Weight: 305 Stats through Nov. 7: 561 snaps, 0.7% pressure rate allowed, 0.8% blown run block rate Williams' playing style is a bit unconventional, and his lack of experience shows throughout games. However, he has plenty of skills that NFL teams covet. Williams' towering frame helps him shadow and shut down pass rushers around the arc of the pocket. His lower-body fluidity and drive strength at the point of attack allows him to gain momentum into blocks as a run blocker. His knee bend must become more consistent throughout reps, and he'll also have moments where he lacks depth in pass protection sets. 16. Darian Mensah , QB, Miami* Height: 6-3 | Weight: 205 Stats through Nov. 7: 212-of-276 passing (76.8%) for 2,694 passing yards and 28 touchdowns to two interceptions; 35 carries for 137 rushing yards (3.9 ypc) and two touchdowns Mensah is a locate-and-loft thrower who has a great sense of true progressions and can string together long stretches of accurate completions. He has great touch on passes, as he can drop throws right into the outstretched arms of targets. Mensah is also unafraid to throw into the teeth of blitzes and make defenses pay for trying to rush his throw plans. He is sufficient enough with his legs to buy time and make throws outside of structure. But Mensah has average velocity when forced to throw into tight windows. And he needs to improve his ball security, as rushers have had success jarring the ball loose from him in the pocket. 17. Jackson Harris , WR, LSU* Height: 6-2 | Weight: 202 Stats through Nov. 7: 47 receptions for 800 receiving yards (17.0 ypc) and seven touchdowns Harris is a sudden, smooth route runner who can execute any branch on the route tree. He can maneuver and control defenders by executing efficient steps and extra body moves. His high-end competitive drive allows him to fight through contact in route stems and create separation at the top of his routes. That competitiveness carries over into his after-the-catch process, where he can turn short-to-intermediate catches into explosive plays because of his instant speed. Harris also has excellent concentration at the catch point. which helps him see the ball into his hands no matter the pass location. 18. Austin Simmons , QB, Missouri* Height: 6-4 | Weight: 220 Stats through Nov. 7: 175-of-283 passing (61.8%) for 2,204 passing yards and 18 touchdowns to two interceptions; 26 carries for 20 rushing yards (0.8 ypc) Simmons has a slight build but is an extremely explosive thrower with A-level arm strength. His baseball pitching background shows, as he has a whippy and violent throwing motion that adds excellent velocity to his passes. There isn't a window on the field that isn't attainable thanks to his arm strength. Simmons is also an anticipatory thrower who is consistent in making "about to be open" throws to targets. He is also capable of executing touch throws and can layer the ball into receivers. Simmons can use his powerful arm as a crutch, as he can be late to some reads and with getting the ball out when pressured. Simmons' physical tools are tantalizing, but the sample size is still very small. 19. Nick Marsh , WR, Indiana* Height: 6-3 | Weight: 210 Stats through Nov. 7: 38 receptions for 669 receiving yards (17.6 ypc) and eight touchdowns Built like a running back, Marsh's separators are his frame, competitiveness and power at the catch point. His strong releases at the line help him work through and steer clear of press coverage prior to making catches. And he's excellent after the catch, turning underneath catches into big gains as defenders bounce off his frame. Marsh is also an outstanding run blocker who isn't afraid of doing the dirty work inside of the box. The one issue with Marsh is that he has yet to develop other tactics to establish and maintain true separation. 20. Jamari Johnson , TE, Oregon Height: 6-5 | Weight: 255 Stats through Nov. 7: 29 receptions for 370 receiving yards (12.8 ypc) and three touchdowns; one carry for two rushing yards (2.0 ypc) and one touchdown Johnson is a big playmaker in the passing game, especially over the middle of the field. He has natural hands and the catch radius to pluck balls outside his frame. As a route runner, Johnson wins with controlled tempos, decisiveness and spatial awareness. He can compete through contact when challenged, but he won't surprise defenders with his top-end speed or suddenness. Johnson also isn't a dynamic threat who can stack up extra yards after the catch that aren't created for him schematically. He isn't overly reliable on single blocks as a run blocker. 21. Trevor Lauck , OT, Iowa Height: 6-5 | Weight: 314 Stats through Nov. 7: 487 snaps, 2.1% pressure rate allowed, 0% blown run block rate Lauck is an old-school, tough offensive tackle. His playing style isn't flashy or glamorous; he simply collects wins in bunches by executing his hand power and physicality. Lauck has upper-tier upper-body strength and hands that are active when initiating contact. His pass sets are a bit unconventional given his average athleticism, but he's savvy with sorting and terminating rush moves. Lauck isn't firm on contact and can get moved off his spot, so he will need to learn to better churn his feet after the initiation process. He could improve his lower-body strength. 22. Lance Heard , OT, Kentucky Height: 6-6 | Weight: 325 Stats through Nov. 7: 572 snaps, 3.1% pressure rate allowed, 1.9% blown run block rate Heard is a physical, wide-framed blocker who uses his natural tools effectively. His physicality is always turned up to the max, as he seeks to destroy anything in his path as a true road grader. He has excellent knockback strength, and defenders jolt back when he's able to get proper hand placement. Heard has average range as a pass protector and quick upfield rushers have had success clearing his near hip to create pathways to pressure passers. He also could be a converted to guard to maximize his strength levels in confined areas. 23. Boubacar Traore , Edge, Notre Dame Height: 6-5 | Weight: 253 Stats through Nov. 7: 30 tackles, four sacks, seven tackles for loss, two forced fumbles, one fumble recovery, one interception for 18 yards, one pass defensed Traore is a long, disruptive presence off the edge. He displays an expansive repertoire of pass-rush moves, including effective speed-to-power transitions and timely spin moves. He has a nonstop motor, routinely accelerates around the rim of pockets and has the bending ability to turn the corner. He is an aware run defender who has the length to stack blockers and keep his vision clean. He must add mass to become firmer at the point of attack and when attempting to set the edge. His counter moves need improvement, but he has the potential to be a reliable No. 2 complementary rusher with more strength. 24. Devan Thompkins , Edge, Alabama Height: 6-5 | Weight: 300 Stats through Nov. 7: 33 tackles, five sacks, 6.5 tackles for loss, one forced fumble Thompkins is a heavy handed, versatile defender capable of rushing from inside and off the edge. With upper-level hand power, he's able to stack and shed from blockers with ease. His overwhelming power at the point of attack helps him create eventual wins as a pass rusher and few blockers can match his power profile. A stout lower half helps him hold up and maintain his gaps. Thompkins can play multiple alignments up-front because of his stout frame and strength levels. 25. LaNorris Sellers , QB, South Carolina* Height: 6-3 | Weight: 238 Stats through Nov. 7: 172-of-274 passing (62.8%) for 2,100 passing yards and 17 touchdowns to seven interceptions; 104 carries for 637 rushing yards (6.1 ypc) and seven touchdowns Sellers is an explosive dual-threat passer with A-level arm power, mobility and body strength. He has a great feel for trajectory and touch on long passes and can make "drop it in the bucket" throws downfield. His compact release helps him fire the ball into condensed windows in intermediate areas. Sellers is also a game changer on designed QB runs and scrambles with his instant acceleration. He is a high-variance passer who makes a mixture of wow throws and turnover-worthy ones. Sellers still plays too programmed and stiff at times. He's a developmental passer who needs to play with more anticipation to unlock his full potential. 26. stories.title: Sources: Philip Rivers set to return to NC State, deal to be finalized Friday
stories.summary: Philip Rivers is set to return to NC State, this time as head football coach, once its trustees finalizes his contract after a meeting Friday, sources said.
stories.detailText: The NC State board of trustees is expected to finalize a contract Friday that will make former NFL quarterback Philip Rivers his alma mater's new head football coach, sources told ESPN on Wednesday. The long-expected hiring of Rivers, who has never been a college coach but is one of the program's most revered former players, is expected to culminate after Friday's meeting, sources told ESPN. Rivers, who played quarterback at NC State from 2000 to 2003, is in his sixth season as coach at St. Michael Catholic High School in Fairhope, Alabama. He built the program from ground up and guided the Cardinals to the state semifinals in 2024 and '25. Sources said the 44-year-old had told NC State that he wanted to finish his current high school season, which ended Friday. In the early stages of the search, Rivers emerged as the favorite to replace Dave Doeren, who was fired Oct. 24. Another former Wolfpack and NFL quarterback, Russell Wilson, was also in discussions about the position. Rivers broke nearly every NC State and ACC record during his career, throwing for 13,484 yards with 95 touchdowns. He led the Wolfpack to four straight bowl games under the Chuck Amato, winning three of them. Amato died last month at 80 years old. Rivers' son, Gunner, committed to play for NC State on Feb. 23. Ranked 168th in the SC Next 300, Gunner Rivers threw for 10,847 yards with 119 touchdowns at St. Michael before his high school career ended due to a knee injury. Philip Rivers played 17 seasons in the NFL, all but one with the Chargers , before retiring after the 2020 season. Last year, he came out of retirement to start three games for the Colts after starter Daniel Jones and backup Riley Leonard were hurt. In January, Rivers interviewed for the Bills ' head coaching vacancy but later removed himself from the search. Information from ESPN's David Hale was used in this report.

stories.title: Dolphins hopeful QB Malik Willis will be back this season
stories.summary: Coach Jeff Hafley said Miami sees Malik Willis as its starter regardless of when he returns from his groin injury.
stories.detailText: MIAMI GARDENS, Fla. -- The Miami Dolphins are hopeful quarterback Malik Willis will return this season after his mandated minimum four-game stay on injured reserve, coach Jeff Hafley said Wednesday, and Willis is expected to remain the team's starter upon his return. Hafley said Willis' MRI showed his groin injury had progressed to his core and the Dolphins' medical team believed he "needed the rest." Willis will seek a second opinion on his injury this week to decide whether or not to undergo surgery, but the Dolphins still see him as their starter, regardless of when he returns. "Our hope is that he'll be back after his four weeks, which in time, if healthy, he'll return," Hafley said. "But he will be the starter when healthy, when he does return. And again, you look back at Malik and you watch him in that last game and you could see it. He couldn't quite move the way he had done early in the year and he was gritting through it and he was toughing through it. He made some plays with his feet in that game to keep plays alive. "But we want him to be healthy so he can play at a high level without risking further injury." Willis received treatment on his groin in each of the past two weeks. It didn't limit his practice participation, but he was noticeably hobbled in last week's loss to the Detroit Lions and was held to single-digit rushing yards for the second game in a row. With Willis sidelined, second-year quarterback Kyle McCord will get his first career start Sunday against the Indianapolis Colts . The Dolphins traded for McCord from the Green Bay Packers in August after the former sixth-round pick led the NFL in passing touchdowns this preseason. Though McCord has primarily run the Dolphins' scout team at practice since his arrival, Hafley said McCord's preseason tape showed desirable traits. "He's got a strong arm, stronger than you think. He sees it well. The ball comes out fast," Hafley said. "He's decisive. He's aggressive. ... Again, he does not have experience in this league and this league is very different, but he does have experience. He has played in a lot of games, but from when I watched him, he's thrown a lot of passes and he does have arm talent and the ball comes out quickly and it'll be interesting to see." The Philadelphia Eagles took McCord in the sixth round of the 2025 NFL draft, after he threw for an FBS-leading 4,779 yards at Syracuse as a senior. He also spent three seasons at Ohio State, going 11-1 as a starter in 2023. McCord said it is his big-game experience in college that gives him confidence heading into the biggest week of his NFL career to date. "It's a blessing, but I think once you get the first play, put on the helmet and get going, I think it'll feel just like football," McCord said of his opportunity. "And I feel like ... that's something that having played those big college games, I think you've been in those moments before my first time playing in a big game. I feel like that's where I'm drawing a lot of confidence from." McCord said that despite his brief time in Miami, he has a full grasp of the playbook and can run "anything [offensive coordinator] Bobby [Slowik] wants to call." According to teammates, he has already shown that grasp at practice this week. Right tackle Austin Jackson said McCord wasn't afraid to correct his teammates at Wednesday's practice, specifically when they weren't lined up appropriately. "I would say he seemed pretty confident today in the huddle, calling the huddle, pretty confident calling the plays out," Jackson said. "There's a couple times the formation was wrong and he actually spotted it out beforehand, which is good. That's something that is big for a quarterback ... the confidence there is the main thing really, at the end of the day, that gets [a quarterback] through it." Left tackle Patrick Paul said McCord has a "moxie" to him that he's excited for people to see Sunday and said he wasn't surprised by his practice habits "because he's a smart player." Paul also said Miami's offensive line has a responsibility to ensure McCord remains comfortable during his first start. "As the O-line, you have to make him feel comfortable," Paul said. "So that's setting a firm pocket and then just off the field, getting with him, talking with him, making sure he's confident, and then just praising him when you can -- just letting him know that you're there and supporting him."

stories.detailText: Staying up to date on NFL injury news is of the utmost importance for fantasy football success. The article below tracks all fantasy-relevant players currently listed on their team's injury report and provides fantasy managers with actionable recommendations as new information rolls in. Check back for updates from Tuesday through Saturday. Don’t forget: Check out the Rotoworld player news feed for all the latest news, notes, and transactions around the league. **UPDATED AS OF WEDNESDAY, NOVEMBER 11 AT 8:08 PM ET** AFC East ◆ Buffalo Bills Dalton Kincaid - TE (ankle) Kincaid was limited to begin Week 10. Impact: Likely none. Kincaid has played through injuries this season largely without issue. Joshua Palmer - WR (hamstring) Palmer managed only seven offensive snaps in Week 8 before departing with an aggravation of the hamstring injury he has battled since Week 4. He was placed on injured reserve. Impact: Not much, honestly. Palmer has played sparingly this season in a situational role, although his absence could leave room for Skylar Bell to be active for the third time this season. ◆ Miami Dolphins De’Von Achane - RB (knee) Achane suffered a torn ACL in the team's Week 3 loss to the Chiefs, ending his season. Impact: Achane's unfortunate season-ending injury creates opportunity for Ollie Gordon and Jaylen Wright . The timing of the injury makes it likely that Achane is able to fully recover before the start of the 2027 regular season. Malik Willis - QB (groin) The Dolphins placed Willis on injured reserve in Week 10. He will be eligible to return in Week 14, but Willis is seeking a second opinion after the injury progressed into his abdomen. Season-ending surgery is possible . Impact : Kyle McCord 's installation as the team's starter hurts all involved. Until we see how McCord fares in this system, only Ollie Gordon is a safe FLEX starter. ◆ New England Patriots Romeo Doubs - WR (shoulder) Doubs was placed on injured reserve following a shoulder injury sustained in Week 6. He will miss the next four games, at minimum. Impact: The Patriots have now played only 33 offensive snaps with both Doubs and A.J. Brown on the field together this season after Doubs was injured on his second offensive snap in Week 6. Brown returned from injured reserve in Week 6 and should have the runway to return WR1 numbers while Doubs remains sidelined. A.J. Brown - WR (knee/ankle) Brown has missed the previous two weeks with a "flare up" in his knee. The team announced Tuesday that he will travel to Germany for Week 10. He was limited to begin the week . Impact: DeMario Douglas , Kyle Williams , Mack Hollins , and Kyle Williams led the team in snaps and routes in the absence of Brown in Week 9, with none of the bunch consistent fantasy producers. Fantasy managers are likely forced to wait until late in the week to get a better sense of whether Brown will return in Week 10. TreVeyon Henderson - RB (illness) Henderson has been sidelined since Week 8 and will not play in Week 10 against the Lions. Impact: See below. Rhamondre Stevenson - RB (knee) Stevenson is reportedly set to miss "a short period of time" with a tendon issue in his knee, per ESPN's Adam Schefter . Impact: An absence from Stevenson could place the team in a dire situation with TreVeyon Henderson also sidelined for an indefinite time, likely leaving Corey Kiiner atop the depth chart for a matchup against the Lions in Germany. Kiner would gain viable FLEX status, should Stevenson miss. Lan Larison is his backup. Hunter Henry - TE (foot) Henry played through this injury in Week 9, and was limited to begin Week 10. Impact : He is a TE2 against the Lions. ◆ New York Jets Garrett Wilson - WR (concussion) Wilson was ruled out for Week 9 Friday after failing to practice all week with a concussion. He was limited to begin Week 10, and head coach Aaron Glenn said he is "very hopeful" that Wilson will play . Impact: Adonai Mitchell could operate as the Jets' No. 1 wide receiver in his albeit volatile downfield role. Omar Cooper - WR (ankle) In Week 9, Cooper injured the same ankle that he hurt earlier this year, but he practiced in a limited capacity to begin Week 10. Impact: Cooper is on track to play and warrants FLEX treatment against the Bills. AFC North ◆ Baltimore Ravens Lamar Jackson - QB (thumb) Jackson returned from an ankle injury in Week 8 and made it all of one offensive snap before suffering a thumb injury that is likely to sideline him for the remainder of the regular season. Impact: Jackson's absence is the biggest hit to the fantasy value of alpha receiver Zay Flowers , who falls to a mid-range WR2 in rest of season rankings. Recent signee Jacoby Brissett is expected to start under center in Week 10 . Tyler Huntley - QB (toe) Huntley suffered a season-ending turf toe injury in the team's Week 8 loss to the Bills. Impact: See above. Durham Smythe - TE (Achilles) Smythe suffered a torn Achilles in the team's Week 4 win over the Titans. His season is done. Impact: It was Matt Hibner who saw the largest increase in snaps following Smythe's departure in Week 4, making it unlikely we see veteran Mark Andrews in a more robust role. ◆ Cincinnati Bengals Andrei Iosivas - WR (thumb) The Bengals placed Iosivas on injured reserve in Week 3 Impact: Wide receivers Colbie Young and Dohnte Meyers will duke it out for the No. 3 wide receiver role for at least the next four weeks. Meyers can be added in 14-team leagues, though his upside is questionable. Erick All - TE (knee) All suffered a torn ACL in Week 7. He was placed on injured reserve Tuesday and will miss the remainder of the regular season. Impact: All loses yet another season in devastating fashion after suffering his third torn ACL. His absence could provide a slight uptick in snap rate and route participation for Mike Gesicki , although he will be a difficult weekly start for as long as both Ja'Marr Chase and Tee Higgins remain healthy. ◆ Cleveland Browns Harold Fannin - TE (groin) Fannin played through the injury in Week 9, but did not enter the box score until overtime. He was limited to begin Week 10. Impact: Likely none. Denzel Boston - WR (toe) Boston did not practice to begin Week 10. Impact: Boston continues to deal with lower-leg injuries, but he played effectively last week. If he cannot face the Texans in Week 10, KC Concepcion and Fannin would benefit. Raheim Sanders - RB (hip) The Browns placed Sanders on injured reserve in Week 6 . Impact: He will be eligible to return after four games missed. ◆ Pittsburgh Steelers Michael Pittman - WR (foot) Pittman was limited on Wednesday before being seen using a scooter in the locker room after practice . It was then revealed that Pittman aggravated his foot injury. The Steelers placed him on injured reserve late in Week 5 . The Steelers did not open his 21-day practice window after their Week 9 bye. Impact: Pittman's potential return could lower Germie Bernard 's target share. Roman Wilson - WR (finger) Wilson departed in the second half of Week 5 with a finger injury and is reportedly looking at a multi-game absence. He was ruled out for Week 6 on Friday and placed on injured reserve on Saturday. Impact: See above. AFC South ◆ Houston Texans Woody Marks - RB (knee) Marks was limited to begin Week 10. Impact: Likely none. Tank Dell - WR (hand/shoulder) Dell was limited to begin Week 10. Impact: Dell led the team with nine targets last week. He may have his work slightly scaled back this week, but he remains FLEX-viable. Marvin Harrison Jr. - WR (hamstring) Harrison was limited to begin Week 10. Impact: Hamstring injuries can be tricky for wide receivers. Kayshon Boutte and Xavier Hutchinson would mildly benefit if Harrison sits. Jaylin Noel - WR (toe) Noel suffered a turf toe injury in Week 7. The Texans placed him on injured reserve in Week 8. He is expected to miss the remainder of the regular season. Impact: Tank Dell and recent acquisition Marvin Harrison Jr. would be in line to benefit. Harrison should be added in 12-team formats. David Montgomery - RB (groin) Head coach DeMeco Ryans said in Week 5 that Montgomery is " week-to-week " with a groin injury. He remains sidelined early in Week 10 . Impact: Woody Marks is a low-end RB2/FLEX. Jawhar Jordan - RB (undisclosed) The Texans placed Jordan on injured reserve in Week 7 . Impact: Jordan prevented Marks from handling a full-time role in Week 6. Dare Ogunbowale will probably do the same while Montgomery is sidelined. Jayden Higgins - WR (knee) Higgins saw his 2026 season taken from him due to a torn ACL suffered in camp. Impact: It's a massive blow to a Texans team that was counting on Higgins taking another step forward in his Sophomore campaign. The team traded for Kayshon Boutte in the wake of the injury and then added Marvin Harrison Jr. in a deal with the Cardinals ahead of Week 6. ◆ Indianapolis Colts Alec Pierce - WR (heel) Pierce aggravated the injury that required offseason surgery in Week 2. The Colts placed him on injured reserve in Week 3 . He will attempt to avoid surgery by rehabbing his injured heel. Head coach Shane Steichen said he is unsure whether Pierce will play again this season . Impact: Tyler Warren is the de facto top option through the air for the remainder of the season. ◆ Jacksonville Jaguars Bayshul Tuten - RB (ankle/foot) Tuten played in Week 9's Thursday Night Football after failing to practice leading up to the game. He did not practice the following Wednesday . Impact: Tuten saw his workload managed in the second half of a blowout win but appears to have escaped without aggravating either injury. Fantasy managers will want to track his status coming out of the mini-bye. Chris Rodriguez - RB (hand) Rodriguez played through the injury in Week 9 and remained limited early in Week 10. Impact : See above. Jakobi Meyers - WR (ankle) Meyers played through the injury in Week 9 and sat out the following Wednesday . Impact: Meyers is a touchdown-dependent FLEX. ◆ Tennessee Titans Carnell Tate - WR (shoulder) Tate remains sidelined following the Titans' Week 9 bye. Impact: This could be consequential. Wan'Dale Robinson would benefit if Tate cannot play in Week 10. Tyjae Spears - RB (knee) As of Week 10 , Spears has been sidelined since Week 7. Impact: Fantasy managers will want to track his status out of the team's Week 9 bye. AFC West ◆ Denver Broncos Jaylen Waddle - WR (concussion) Waddle suffered a concussion in the team's Week 9 win over the Panthers. Impact: The team's Week 10 bye should afford Waddle enough time to return without missing a game. RJ Harvey - RB (knee) Harvey popped on the injury report Thursday with a knee injury and was ruled out for Week 8 on Friday. He was placed on injured reserve Saturday and will miss the next four weeks, at minimum. Impact: Jonah Coleman is an RB2, operating as the team's starter. ◆ Kansas City Chiefs Patrick Mahomes - QB (elbow) Mahomes suffered an elbow injury to his throwing arm in the team's Week 9 win over the Jets. He is practicing in full for Week 10 against the Falcons. Impact: Pain management could lead to reduced throwing volume for Mahomes. Backup quarterback Justin Fields ( neck ) is practicing in full as well. Tyquan Thornton - WR (ankle) Thornton suffered a devastating ankle injury due to a hip-drop tackle in Week 4. He is reportedly set to undergo surgery within the week and will miss 12-16 weeks. Impact: The team has lost all ability to attack downfield without Thornton, meaning our fantasy interest should be confined to those with expected volume. ◆ Las Vegas Raiders The Raiders emerged from their Week 9 loss to the 49ers absent any fantasy-relevant injuries. ◆ Los Angeles Chargers David Njoku - TE (fibula) Njoku is reportedly set to see his 21-day practice window opened in the coming days. He was limited to begin Week 9 before being listed as doubtful . Impact: Minimal. The Chargers have been the most disappointing offense in the league through the halfway point of the season. Ladd McConkey - WR (back) McConkey reportedly experienced back spasms during warmups for Week 9 and ultimately did not play . Impact: McConkey now gets a long week of preparation ahead of a Monday Night Football contest against the Ravens. Fantasy managers will want to monitor his level of participation in practice closely in the coming days. He would be a viable WR3 if active. Justin Herbert - QB (left hand) Herbert injured his non-throwing hand in Week 9. Impact: Likely minimal. NFC East ◆ Dallas Cowboys Jake Ferguson - TE (ankle) Ferguson departed the team's Week 9 win with an ankle injury. Head coach Brian Schottenheimer said Monday that the veteran tight end is "expected to miss time." Impact: Brevin Span-Ford is on hand to handle primary tight end duties. He is not a recommended streaming option outside of the deepest leagues. George Pickens - WR (hamstring) Pickens missed Week 9 with a hamstring injury. He was limited to begin Week 10. Impact: Fantasy managers will want to monitor his status ahead of a Week 10 meeting with the 49ers. CeeDee Lamb could be in line for another massive target share should Pickens miss. Ryan Flournoy would be a starting FLEX. Malik Davis - RB (hip) Davis was placed on injured reserve and will miss the remainder of the 2026 season. Impact: The Cowboys released both Jaydon Blue and Phil Mafah at roster cuts and now have only Emari Demercado on the active roster behind starter Javonte Williams . Expect Israel Abanikanda to be elevated to the active roster from the practice squad for Week 2, while Williams appears likely to see all the work he can handle against the Commanders. Williams is a locked-in RB1. ◆ New York Giants Jaxson Dart - QB (knee) Dart injured his MCL, PCL and meniscus on the team's first possession of Monday Night Football against the Rams. He will undergo surgery to address the MCL and meniscus and miss the rest of the regular season. Giants head coach John Harbaugh said it is possible for Dart to return in the postseason, although this is unlikely. Impact: Backup Jameis Winston was benched in favor of recent acquisition J.J. McCarthy in the second half of their loss to the Saints. Head coach John Harbaugh confirmed McCarthy as the starter for Week 7. Cam Skattebo - RB (hamstring) Skattebo will play in Week 10 after sitting out in Week 9. Impact: Skattebo is back in the RB2 ranks against the Commanders. J.J. McCarthy - QB (hip) McCarthy was in and out of the lineup in Week 9 after a painful hip pointer. He will play in Week 10 against the Commanders. Impact: McCarthy is QB2-viable on Thursday night. ◆ Philadelphia Eagles Saquon Barkley - RB (back/hamstring) Barkley should continue to play through the ailments after being active in Week 9. Impact: Barkley is a volume-based RB1/2. Dameon Pierce - RB (undisclosed) Pierce was injured on a kick return in the fourth quarter of the team's Week 7 loss to the Cowboys. He was placed on injured reserve the following Wednesday . Impact: See above. DeVonta Smith - WR (hamstring) Smith has repeatedly aggravated the hamstring strain he initially injured in August. Smith was ruled out for Week 7 on Saturday, and as of early in Week 9, he remains sidelined . Both Smith and Dontayvion Wicks were ruled out for Week 9 on Friday. Impact: Wide receivers Dontayvion Wicks (ankle) and Britain Covey (knee) remain sidelined as well. All three could be held out through the Eagles' Week 10 bye. Tight end Dallas Goedert and Makai Lemon benefit. Tank Bigsby - RB (core) See above. Impact: See above. Jalen Hurts - QB (blood clots) Team doctors discovered a blood clot in Hurts' calf. He was ruled out for Week 6 and could be looking at an extended absence. He was placed on injured reserve on Saturday after more clots were found in his lungs. Impact: Hurts is currently sidelined indefinitely. Tanner McKee enters the starting lineup under center following the release of Andy Dalton. The Philadelphia offense could be in trouble in the immediate future considering the sheer number of injuries. Will Shipley - RB (foot) Shipley reportedly suffered a partial tear of the plantar fascia in his foot in Week 5. He is expected to miss multiple weeks. Impact: See above. ◆ Washington Commanders Terry McLaurin - WR (knee) McLaurin suffered a season-ending patellar tendon rupture in Week 6. Impact: Stefon Diggs will likely serve as the de facto No. 1 wide receiver moving forward. Jaylin Lane - WR (ankle) Lane suffered a dislocated ankle and fracture in Week 4 and is likely done for the season. Impact: Minimal. Lane was primarily a special teams contributor. Jacory Croskey-Merritt - RB (groin) Croskey-Merritt was unable to practice this week and ruled out for Week 6 against the 49ers. The team placed him on injured reserve on Saturday. Impact: Expect Rachaad White to fill in as the primary rusher, with Austin Ekeler on hand to soak up primary change of pace duties. White can be started as a viable FLEX option while Ekeler is likely best left on fantasy benches. Jeremy McNichols - RB (foot) McNichols suffered a foot injury in Week 8 and was placed on injured reserve in Week 9. Impact: Rachaad White and veteran Austin Ekeler are suddenly the only two healthy backs on the Washington roster, neither of whom is an overly exciting fantasy option on a struggling offense. White is the preferred option and could be started as a viable FLEX, should McNichols miss time. Treylon Burks - WR (foot) Burks did not play in Week 9. He was cleared to play in Week 10's Thursday Night Football game despite logging on limited practice this week, on Tuesday . Impact: Burks could be a decoy. Antonio Williams is limited to FLEX status until he proves otherwise. NFC North ◆ Chicago Bears Kyle Monangai - RB (thumb/toe) Head coach Ben Johnson labeled Monangai as " day-to-day " with a thumb injury suffered in Week 4, but he was later revealed to have suffered a turf toe injury as well. Monangai remains sidelined as of Week 9's Wednesday practice. He did not play in Week 9. Impact: D'Andre Swift is an RB1, should Monangai miss another game. Roschon Johnson can be stashed. Cole Kmet - TE (knee) Kmet suffered a season-ending knee injury in the team's Thursday Night Football win over the Patriots. Impact: Expect Sam Roush to serve as the team's TE2 for the remainder of the season, while second-year tight end Colston Loveland should continue his recent ascension back into TE1 territory. ◆ Detroit Lions Jared Goff - QB (chest) Goff's play may have been impacted by the injury in-game last week, though it is tough to say for sure. Hopefully he upgrades to full participation on Thursday. He was limited on Wednesday . Impact: Likely none. Amon-Ra St. Brown - WR (ribs) St. Brown was limited on Wednesday after playing through the injury in Week 9. Impact : None. Isiah Pacheco - RB (back) Pacheco was placed on injured reserve to start the season. General Manager Brad Holmes said he "hopes Pacheco returns this season." Impact: Well, that doesn't sound great. There appears to be something more insidious going on with Pacheco's back than initially thought. Lions coach Dan Campbell said running backs Jacob Saylors and Sione Vaki could split touches behind Jahmyr Gibbs . Saylors appears to be the first player up. Gibbs handled an absurd 34 opportunities, of 37 total running back opportunities, in the team's Week 1, overtime win over the Saints ◆ Green Bay Packers Josh Jacobs - RB (finger) Jacobs suffered a fractured finger in the team's Week 9 win over the Patriots. He will miss two-to-three weeks after undergoing surgery . Impact: Kaleb Johnson is reportedly the first in line for lead back duties in his absence. Jayden Reed - WR (neck) Reed suffered a scary-looking neck injury that required stabilization in the team's Week 2 win over the Jets. Packers head coach Matt LaFleur said on Tuesday that it is " way too early " to determine whether Reed will play again in 2026. That said, he was not placed on injured reserve ahead of their Week 3 contest. He will reportedly undergo surgery . Impact: Beyond the football implications, it is good to hear Reed avoided any life-altering injuries in Week 2. Skyy Moore and Bo Melton are likely to soak up additional snaps, although volume is most likely to concentrate on Christian Watson , Matthew Golden , and Tucker Kraft . Chris Brooks - RB (ankle) Brooks suffered an ankle injury in the team's Week 4 win over the Buccaneers. The Packers designated him to return from injured reserve in Week 9. Impact: Brooks will rotate in on passing downs upon his return for pass-protection duties. ◆ Minnesota Vikings Kyler Murray - QB (hamstring) Murray was reportedly “slowed” by a hamstring injury in the team’s Week 8 loss to the Lions and is undergoing further tests to identify the severity. Those tests revealed a Grade 2 hamstring strain, which is likely to sideline the newly anointed backup quarterback for 3-4 weeks. Impact: Murray can be dropped. Carson Wentz ( ankle ) is also ailing. T.J. Hockenson - TE (wrist/chest) Hockenson did not practice on Wednesday . Impact: Jordan Addison could benefit if Hockenson cannot play in Week 10. Don’t forget: Check out the Rotoworld player news feed for all the latest news, notes, and transactions around the league. NFC South ◆ Atlanta Falcons Brian Robinson - RB (hamstring) Robinson was placed on injured reserve on Saturday. Impact: In a shocking development, Robinson went from limited showings in practice with a questionable designation for Week 9 to injured reserve, with the potential that the veteran backup aggravated his ailment sometime during practice to end the week. He will miss the next four games, at minimum. Khalil Herbert should continue as the top change-of-pace option behind Bijan Robinson , the former of whom is not fantasy-viable. Zachariah Branch - WR (hamstring) Branch was ruled out for Week 9 against the Bengals early in the week. He remains sidelined in Week 10. Impact: Drake London, Bijan Robinson and Kyle Pitts should continue dominating targets. ◆ Carolina Panthers Jonathan Brooks - RB (groin) Brooks aggravated the groin injury that forced him to miss the end of camp. The Panthers placed him on injured reserve in Week 3. The Panthers designated him to return in Week 10 . He is practicing in full. Impact: Chuba Hubbard likely remains in the volume-driven RB1 tier. Brooks is entirely unproven and does not necessarily need to be stashed in 12-team leagues. ◆ New Orleans Saints Travis Etienne - RB (hamstring) The Saints opened Etienne's 21-day practice window in Week 10. He was limited on Wednesday . Impact: Audric Estime is a starting FLEX if Etienne sits out in Week 10. ◆ Tampa Bay Buccaneers Jalen McMillan - WR (knee) McMillan suffered a sprained PCL in his first game action of the season in Week 3. The team placed him on injured reserve Monday, with an expected absence of 6-8 weeks. Impact: Not much change considering he made his season debut in Week 3, although rookie Ted Hurst should remain in the starting lineup. NFC West ◆ Arizona Cardinals Jeremiyah Love - RB (ankle) The team placed Love on injured reserve after yet another ankle injury sustained in Week 8. Impact: Bam Knight (concussion) resumed practicing in Week 10. Tyler Allgeier likely returns to a receiving/rotational rushing role. Jalen Brooks - WR (wrist) Brooks had emergency surgery on his wrist and will miss the remainder of the regular season. Impact: The team signed veteran Zay Jones Tuesday in an associated move. Expect volume to continue to remain heavily concentrated on Michael Wilson and Trey McBride . Elijah Higgins is notable for DFS purposes. Gardner Minshew - QB (elbow) Minshew is feared to have torn his UCL in the team's Week 9 loss to the Seahawks. Impact: Minshew appears likely to be placed on injured reserve in the coming days, leaving rookie Carson Beck to start under center for the remainder of the season. Michael Wilson - WR (neck) Wilson suffered a neck injury in Week 9 that will end his 2026 season. Impact: The Cardinals are now without their starting quarterback, second-string quarterback, alpha wide receiver, secondary and tertiary wide receiver, and starting running back as they head into the second half of a lost season. Trey McBride should soak up all the volume he can handle, with that volume now coming from rookie Carson Beck . ◆ Los Angeles Rams Terrance Ferguson - TE (hamstring) Ferguson appeared to be on track to be activated from injured reserve after logging a full practice to end the week, but was ruled out for Week 9 with a new hamstring injury. He will miss multiple games . Impact: Fantasy managers will have to continue to wait for the return of Ferguson. Davante Adams - WR (hamstring) The Rams placed Adams on i njured reserve with a ruptured hamstring tendon. He underwent surgery in Week 8. The team is targeting a Week 13 return . Impact: The Rams will employ run-heavy game plans in the coming weeks. Puka Nacua - WR (knee/toe) Nacua suffered PCL and MCL sprains, plus a turf toe injury, on the final play from scrimmage in the team's Week 9 win over the Commanders. Nacua could return in Weeks 14 or 15, and he will not be placed on injured reserve due to transaction limits . Impact: See above. ◆ San Francisco 49ers Mike Evans - WR (Achilles) Evans aggravated his Achilles injury in Week 6 and is expected to " miss some time ." He remains sidelined early in Week 10. Impact: Evans will likely miss this week's game. Deebo Samuel - WR (hamstring) Samuel suffered a hamstring injury in the team's Week 5 win over the Seahawks. He resumed practicing in Week 10 and told reporters he is " ready " to play. Impact: Samuel would return to the high-end FLEX tier if active. Christian Kirk - WR (knee) Kirk was limited on Wednesday . He was ruled out for Week 9 on Friday and placed on injured reserve on Saturday. Impact: None. De’Zhaun Stribling - WR (ankle) Stribling suffered an ankle injury in the team's Week 1 win over the Rams. The 49ers placed him on injured reserve in Week 2 after he underwent surgery to repair a deltoid ligament tear. He is expected to return in 10 weeks. stories.title: Eagles-Giants Film Review: The defense gave us something worth discussing
stories.summary: All-22 analysis from Philadelphia’s Week 9 loss.
stories.detailText: PHILADELPHIA, PENNSYLVANIA - NOVEMBER 08: Zack Baun #53 of the Philadelphia Eagles sacks J.J. McCarthy #18 of the New York Giants during the second quarter at Lincoln Financial Field on November 08, 2026 in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. (Photo by Caleb Bowlin/Getty Images) | Getty Images This was better. Not perfect, and there are still moments in the secondary that make me want to pause the film and stare at the ceiling and wonder what is going on, but it was better. The Eagles stopped the run and generated some pass rush. Allowing 19 points and 243 yards should be enough to keep you competitive. Apparently, that is asking too much of this offense . The Giants averaged 3.8 yards per play, and Devin Singletary finished with 31 yards on 21 carries. The Eagles recorded six sacks. This group will still fight under Vic Fangio. I think that matters, even in a season that has become this frustrating. The defense couldn’t do much more. The defense cannot save this offense every week. With the NFL trade deadline now behind us, I am increasingly interested in who should be part of the next version of this team. Some players are worth getting excited about, and some positions need serious attention. Let’s get into it. Defense This was Zack Baun’s best game for a few weeks. He was everywhere against the run and good in coverage, too. His recent struggles have made it easy to forget just how good he can be when he sees things clearly and gets to attack. On this rep, he reads the run immediately, gets into the backfield, and finishes. There is no hesitation. It’s a lot easier to play linebacker when your defensive linemen aren’t slanting away from the run and letting a guard get to the second level immediately. Baun finished with seven combined tackles, three tackles for loss, and two sacks. Those numbers match the film, but I also thought the defensive line did a better job of allowing him to play like this. The linebackers have spent too much time dealing with blockers in recent weeks. Here, Baun can trust what he sees and go. This was much more like it. Eagles' Defense All22 thread vs. Giants. 1) This was the best Zack Baun game for a few weeks. He was everywhere against the run and good in coverage, too. He's struggled like everyone at times over the past couple of weeks, but it's easy to forget just how good he is. Here he… pic.twitter.com/zkm5Wmp7Vd — Jonny Page (@JonnyPage9) November 10, 2026 Unfortunately, we also got an early reminder that the secondary still has issues. The Giants repeatedly attacked the quarters side of Cover 6 from 3×1. Cover 6 combines quarters coverage on one side with Cover 2 on the other. Against this distribution, the Giants send the outside receiver vertically to take the outside corner deep and run a sail route into the intermediate space underneath. The Eagles do not distribute those routes cleanly. Tariq Woolen carries the vertical, Andrew Mukuba cannot get across to the sail, and there is not enough help underneath. The result is a receiver sitting in a huge amount of space on third down. This is pretty poor for a Fangio’ defense. I am not going to pretend I know the exact check because there are a lot of variables. Depending on how the Eagles coach this, the answer could involve Mukuba getting across sooner or Woolen coming off the vertical with help over the top. But somebody has to account for the intermediate route. The receiver cannot simply disappear from the defense’s rules. We have seen far too much uncertainty like this all season. 2) Back to back 3rd and long, the Giants wrecked the Eagles' coverage rules. The Eagles struggled to distribute routes against 3×1 in Cover 6. On consecutive third downs, the Giants flooded the quarters side, clearing the outside corner vertically and leaving the intermediate… pic.twitter.com/UWpcZCEKJJ — Jonny Page (@JonnyPage9) November 10, 2026 Well, one final mention for Jordan Davis. Goodbye, big man. The run defense will miss you. A healthy Davis is still one of the best run defenders you will watch, and this rep shows why. Few players his size can make a play like this. The combination of his size and movement ability is unusual, and it has real value. I was not Davis’ biggest fan early in his career, but he turned it around and has played well for a couple of years now. He deserves credit for that, and he deserves our thanks. It feels strange watching the Eagles trade away a young player they drafted because the team is not competitive. That is a fairly miserable place to be. I think they were right to accept the deal. The value was too good to pass up for a player who doesn’t consistently affect the quarterback as a pass rusher. Yes, he had a sack in this game. That does not change the broader evaluation of his pass-rush contribution. You can appreciate how good he became against the run and understand the decision to move him. Both things are true. Personally, I will miss him as a character on this team. Good luck, JD! 3) Well, I had to give him one final mention. Goodbye, Jordan Davis; this run defense will miss you. The Eagles got a great deal and were right to accept it, but a healthy Jordan Davis is still one of the best run defenders you will watch. It still feels weird to watch us trade… pic.twitter.com/PxOH0IMoXF — Jonny Page (@JonnyPage9) November 10, 2026 And here is the same coverage problem on the following third down. This time it is third-and-12, and the Giants attack the quarters side again. The outside receiver clears the corner vertically, the second receiver stops short and occupies the underneath defender, and the inside receiver runs the sail beyond the sticks. It is a simple way to put different levels of the coverage under stress, and the Eagles make it look far too easy. I am much more inclined to put this one on Mukuba. Based on the receiver splits and how the other defenders react, I struggle to see how the Eagles can draw this up without asking him to get across to that route. He is so late that the quarterback does not have a difficult decision. The underneath defender has committed to the short route, and the outside cornerback has to take the deep route. There may be details in the coaching rules that we cannot see, but the repeated outcome is the problem. Two third downs, the same basic idea, and another open receiver. Mukuba is becoming a real concern for me. Safety needs to be a serious priority next offseason because the Eagles cannot keep having these issues in their coverage structure. 4) Here's the following 3rd down. The Giants attack the quarters side of the Eagles’ Cover 6 on 3rd-and-12 once again. The outside clears the outside CB, the 2 stops short and occupies the underneath defender, and the inside receiver runs the sail. Once again, Mukuba can’t get… pic.twitter.com/tr1kyfimwY — Jonny Page (@JonnyPage9) November 10, 2026 There was some pass-rush juice this week! One reason was that the Eagles stopped the run on early downs and earned opportunities to attack the quarterback. That matters. It is much easier to get into your rush plan when the offense can’t keep threatening you with an efficient run game. This stunt involving Jonathan Greenard and Baun works well here, and Baun finishes the play against J.J. McCarthy. The Giants end up with a third-down sack rather than another easy completion. This defense did not play soft. It created negative plays and forced the Giants to settle for field goals. A competent offense would have had a chance to win this game. 5) The Eagles had some pass rush juice this week! I think one big reason was their ability to stop the run on early downs, which let them get after the QB as they did here. The stunt with Greenard and Baun works well, and Baun cleans up McCarthy. The defense didn't play soft… pic.twitter.com/QWjTtGCZp2 — Jonny Page (@JonnyPage9) November 10, 2026 I feel like I have written about this problem every week for a month. An opponent puts a tight end across from Quinyon Mitchell and gets its best receiver matched up inside against someone the Eagles would surely rather protect. We have seen versions of it with Tet McMillan and Stefon Diggs. Now it is Malik Nabers against Kenny Moore II. No elaborate motion sequence or clever switch release is required here. The Giants line up and get the matchup. Mitchell is outside, and the ball goes to the receiver they want against the defender they want. I understand the Eagles cannot dictate every matchup, and moving people around has consequences elsewhere. But how many times do we need to watch the same basic issue before there is a better answer? Is there no world in which we ask Quinyon to travel with an opposing receiver when he lines up in the slot? Mitchell’s individual coverage chart was much better this week. He was excellent. That is good. He can also play well while an opponent finds ways to attack other parts of the secondary. The Eagles have to make those other matchups harder to access. 6) Every single week. A team will line up their tight end over Quinyon Mitchell and their best receiver against an Eagles safety in the slot. It has happened every single week for the past month. Tet McMillan, Stefon Diggs, and now Malik Nabers. The offense has no motion,… pic.twitter.com/fWO3z58DsL — Jonny Page (@JonnyPage9) November 10, 2026 This is an excellent third-and-four rep, and it starts with tight coverage. McCarthy does not have the easy answer he wants, which gives Moro Ojomo time to drive the blocker back into the pocket. That interior push takes away the quarterback’s space and pushes him toward Greenard coming around the edge. Greenard gets the sack, but Ojomo does most of the work. Ojomo had a really good game. He is one of the highest-effort players on this team and one of the few defenders who looks like he is playing his best football right now. The individual pressure chart credited Greenard with five pressures and Ojomo with three, but this is a good example of why the final number doesn’t tell the whole story of a rush. Now that the trade deadline has passed, I am interested in what happens next with Ojomo. Will we see an extension? I hope the Eagles are thinking seriously about his future here. With Davis gone, the decisions about the interior defensive line become even more interesting. Ojomo is giving them plenty of reasons to keep him around. I didn’t want to extend Ojomo with Jordan Davis and Jalen Carter already paid, but now I’m not 7) Excellent play on 3rd and 4. The coverage is really tight, and Ojomo rushes extremely well by bull-rushing the quarterback back into Greenard coming around the edge. Greenard gets the sack, but this play is made by Ojomo, who had a really good game. I wonder if we will see… pic.twitter.com/5wf2P8bc1J — Jonny Page (@JonnyPage9) November 10, 2026 Jalen Carter had another up-and-down game, but there was still the rep where he reminded you what he can do. The Eagles use the front to force the Giants to shift their protection left, giving Carter a one-on-one opportunity against the right guard. That is a matchup you expect him to win, and he does. This is the kind of situation the Eagles should want to create. Make the protection account for the rest of the front and give your most talented interior rusher a chance to beat one blocker. Carter produces the sack and forces a fumble, although the Giants recover it. I still want more consistency across his game, but the ability to change a possession is clearly there. 8) Jalen Carter had another up-and-down game, but as always, he had one excellent play where he showed you what he can do. The Eagles do a good job with their front, forcing the Giants to shift left and giving Carter a one-on-one matchup against the right guard. This is a… pic.twitter.com/zogCyDhKd4 — Jonny Page (@JonnyPage9) November 10, 2026 Phew. Baun again. What a blitz. He bursts past the running back and gets to McCarthy before the quarterback can find a solution. This is the version of the defense I enjoy watching. An edge defender drops, a linebacker blitzes, and the coverage behind it looks coordinated. Call me an old-school Fangio fan, but I would like to see more of these standard quarters (or Quads if you live in the Fangio world) looks. It feels as though we spend so much time discussing Cover 3, Cover 6, and Cover 8, while some of the cleanest football comes when the Eagles play quarters behind a pressure like this. The rush changes who the protection has to deal with, and the coverage rules look much clearer on this snap. This combination of pressure and coverage worked beautifully, and Baun finished it outstandingly. 9) Phew, Zack Baun again. What a blitz. He bursts past the running back and gets to the quarterback. To me, this is the Eagles at their best on defense. I'm shocked we don't see more standard quads anymore. It feels like everything is Cover 3, 6, or 8. Call me an old-school… pic.twitter.com/sWe0kBE0Oy — Jonny Page (@JonnyPage9) November 10, 2026 Fangio also tried to use Cooper DeJean differently against the run. Watching this live, I assumed DeJean was playing nickel. He is actually a safety in the box with the Eagles in base personnel, meaning they show a straightforward single-high structure before the snap. That is unusual for this defense. I liked it. Fangio clearly knows the Eagles have to do more to stop the run, and this adjustment helps here. It is worth acknowledging when he changes something, especially after the criticism of the run defense in recent weeks. The Giants’ running backs combined for 51 yards on 24 carries. Whatever issues remained elsewhere, the Eagles did a much better job of preventing the Giants’ running game from getting going. 10) Fangio clearly made an effort to use DeJean differently at safety against the run, and you can see it worked here. Watching this play live, I assumed DeJean was in the nickel, but the Eagles are in base! DeJean is just a safety in the box, which means the Eagles are in… pic.twitter.com/58JgUF7fw0 — Jonny Page (@JonnyPage9) November 10, 2026 However, the communication problems did not go away. The Giants use late motion and a switch release here, changing the route distribution the secondary has to sort out. Give the offense credit for creating a more difficult picture. The Eagles still have to handle it better. I cannot say for certain whether this is on Mukuba or Mitchell. That uncertainty adds to the frustration because the coverage doesn’t look connected, and we keep seeing plays where defenders seem to have different expectations about who should take which route. Coverage issues seemed to follow Mukuba around in this game, which is worrying. I do not want to put every breakdown on one young safety, but I can’t ignore the pattern. This secondary needs dependable communication, and too often it looks as though the players are trying to work out the answer after the receiver is already open. 11) However, some things don't change this season. As said earlier, the communication is just off. Bring back Reed Blankenship. Something's not right with this secondary. Yes, the Giants do a good job with late motion and a switch release, but the Eagles just have to be better.… pic.twitter.com/RpPRBRSpu3 — Jonny Page (@JonnyPage9) November 10, 2026 DeJean also continues to have a coverage rep each week, which frustrates me. Nabers is excellent, but DeJean has outside leverage and inside help here. His job is to protect the outside, and he allows the inside stem to compromise that positioning. He bites inside and opens his hips too early. Once Nabers gets back outside him, DeJean has to spin to recover, which costs him vision and allows separation. The issue is his response to the route with the leverage and help available. He needs to stay square and make Nabers work hard to get outside. He makes this much harder for himself than he needs to. 12) Cooper DeJean can't avoid making a bad play every week in coverage. This is a rough one. Nabers is excellent, but he has clear outside leverage, inside help, and can't be beaten like this. Hites on the inside stem and opens his hips too early. Nabers gets outside him,… pic.twitter.com/re9Hol5uPQ — Jonny Page (@JonnyPage9) November 10, 2026 Let’s finish with another good play against the run. Ojomo bursts off the snap and blows through the left tackle, allowing Jeremiah Trotter Jr. to get through untouched. Trotter can attack the ball rather than deal with a blocker before he reaches the runner. That was one of the biggest differences in this game. Trotter and Baun both played well, and the defensive line deserves credit for helping them. Trotter finished with 10 combined tackles and three tackles for loss. I liked his performance, but this clip also shows why evaluating linebackers solely by the tackle total misses so much. Ojomo creates the opportunity. Trotter takes it. The front works together. Ojomo had multiple reps like this, and I thought his game was better than the basic stat sheet suggested. These are the plays I want to see more of over the remaining weeks. Let’s see more young defenders winning their assignments and making the players around them better. 13) Last one, let's end with another good play against the run. Ojomo bursts off the snap and blows through the left tackle, which allows Jeremiah Trotter to get through untouched. Both Trotter and Baun were good in this game, but one of the big differences was the play of the… pic.twitter.com/Nl9mXppfOe — Jonny Page (@JonnyPage9) November 10, 2026 Final Thoughts This was a better defensive performance. There was real resistance against the run and some life in the pass rush. The Eagles still fight under Fangio, and I do not think this film looks like a defense that has stopped caring. The offense gave them very little support again. That does not excuse the third-down coverage failures or the two consecutive second-half scoring drives that consumed more than 14 minutes. There is plenty to correct, especially in the secondary. I do not know whether Fangio will be back next season (I imagine it is unlikely), but whoever coaches this group needs more reliable play at safety and far fewer communication breakdowns. With the deadline behind us, my attention is shifting toward the players who can help the next version of this team. Trotter’s development matters. Mukuba needs to improve before we can consider him a starter next year. Ojomo is playing football that makes me want him here for the long term, and I will be watching what the Eagles do about his contract. The defense gave us something worth discussing this week. It just cannot keep rescuing an offense that barely gives it a chance. Thank you for reading! I’d love to hear your thoughts, so feel free to comment below and ask any questions.
