stories.title: Cardinals to start rookie QB Carson Beck against Rams
stories.summary: The Cardinals will start their third quarterback in three weeks, with rookie Carson Beck getting the nod for Sunday's home game against the Rams.
stories.detailText: TEMPE, Ariz. -- Arizona Cardinals rookie quarterback Carson Beck will make his NFL debut Sunday against the Los Angeles Rams , coach Mike LaFleur said Wednesday. Quarterback Gardner Minshew II was placed on injured reserve Tuesday after suffering a UCL injury in his throwing arm Sunday at Seattle , paving the way for Beck to get his first career start. Beck, a third-round pick by Arizona, spent the first eight weeks as the Cardinals' emergency third quarterback and was inactive on game day. He was the backup against the Seahawks after Arizona traded Jacoby Brissett to Baltimore . "Obviously having gone from emergency quarterback at the beginning of the season to last week being the backup to now being the starter, I mean, it's been a crazy season," Beck said. "It's really been a welcome to the NFL season that just getting introduced to what the league is and what it can be." LaFleur said Beck, who played in 55 games over six seasons at Georgia and Miami , won't be fazed by the moment. "I know this isn't too big for him," LaFleur said. "Go have some fun, man. Go let it sling." Beck's last start came in January in the CFP National Championship game, which Miami lost to Indiana 27-21. The game before, Beck led the Hurricanes to a win over Ole Miss in the CFP quarterfinals at the Fiesta Bowl at State Farm Stadium, where he'll play Sunday. "Obviously that was a super cool moment for me, probably my favorite game I've ever played in," Beck said. "So there's some good moments I've already had in that stadium, but it'll be really cool to walk in that stadium and know what's at stake and what's to come on Sunday for sure." LaFleur said he wants to see Beck continue what he has been doing in practice and treat each play individually. "You never really know until you get to the live bullets on Sunday, but just the way he goes about his business ... have all the confidence that he's ready to roll," the coach said. LaFleur said Beck "will not be scared" of letting it fly in his NFL debut. As the backup, Beck doubled his workload running the scout team offense, according to quarterbacks coach Matt Schaub. "He can translate those into getting himself prepared, moving around the pocket, not just going through the motions, and he's really diligent on that and just going through his process, which he's been doing all year, but it's just those physical reps," Schaub said. Schaub said he saw a change in Beck's demeanor with the increased reps. "He's a confident kid by nature, so he's reserved, but I mean he's been what he's been since he's been here," Schaub said. "And so it's been good to see him getting his workload ramped up, especially he had some little injury situation in camp, so he lost some reps and some experience and just development there, but he's picked back up and so we like where he's at." Beck was asked about his growth this season and mentioned the difference in the playbook: "You go all the way back to when I first got here and rookie minicamp, OTAs, I mean, just trying to say a whole playcall in the huddle is not the easiest thing ever. I did a little bit at Georgia. We had pretty long playcalls. Miami, a little bit shorter, but we had a couple long ones. "But again, just in that standpoint of things, looking at it, being able to operate and get in and out of the huddle, communicate well, I think that's a huge thing that obviously I've got a ton of practice at. So it's something that I've definitely got better at." LaFleur credited Beck's college experience for helping him prepare to start. "He's been a pro since he's been here," LaFleur said. "He puts in the exact amount of work that he needs. And then from a physical standpoint, he'll obviously get 100% of the reps." Beck said sitting for three years at Georgia "prepared me for this -- of how to handle yourself like a pro when you are on the sideline, when you are the backup, how to still prepare like you are the starter. You have to learn those things. "That's a skill that you have to, through trial and error, figuring out what kind of schedule do I want to have for myself so that when you do get your opportunity, you're not doing anything new, you're just doing the same stuff and now you're obviously just going out there and actually the guy doing it." Beck will be throwing to a number of familiar receivers he worked with on the practice squad before he was the No. 2 quarterback last week. Arizona's currently active receiving corps of Simi Fehoko , Reggie Virgil and Devin Duvernay has a combined eight catches this season. However, Beck's tight end corps of Trey McBride , Elijah Higgins and Teagan Quitoriano has 94 combined. LaFleur said playing in his first NFL game with receivers he knows well will be beneficial to Beck. "He knows how these guys move and he knows the indicators that they're given," LaFleur said. "So, he sees them in the huddle, albeit with no one watching. I mean it's going to be a little bit different on Sunday, but absolutely." LaFleur made it official Wednesday that Minshew needs surgery and will miss the rest of the season. With their quarterback room depleted, the Cardinals added veteran Josh Johnson and Joey Aguilar to the active roster Tuesday. LaFleur worked with Johnson in 2020 with the 49ers and in 2021 with the Jets . LaFleur said Arizona was interested in Aguilar during the draft process, but after selecting Beck and with a stocked quarterback room of veterans, the Cardinals didn't have room for another signal-caller. "So, it just ran its course at that point, had some interest in him," LaFleur said. "When all this unfolded, it was an easy deal for us."

stories.title: Chicago Bears-Tampa Bay Bucs stockwatch: Caleb down, Devin Bush up
stories.summary: In his weekly stock watch, @SamHouseholder reviews the Bucs game and which players performed well.
stories.detailText: CHICAGO, ILLINOIS - NOVEMBER 8: Devin Bush #12 of the Chicago Bears hypes up his teammates before the game against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers at Soldier Field on November 8, 2026 in Chicago, Illinois. (Photo by Todd Rosenberg/Getty Images) | Getty Images The cliché of the week for Chicago Bears fans is “the bye week is coming at the perfect time.” The team is struggling with injuries. And their weaknesses nearly cost them the game against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers. We know injuries ravage the secondary, which is also the weakest part of the defense. The running backs are banged up, to say the least. The Bears have also turned the ball over way more than they did in 2025. Plus, they’ve been penalized a lot, too. All that said, though, they’re still 7-2 and currently in first place in the division, despite their two losses being to division opponents. And the schedule gets tougher from here. The Bears need to have both a productive and restful bye week in order to finish out the season, correct the things they can and secure a playoff berth for the second-straight year. Let’s get into a review of the Bucs game. Stock up Jaylon Johnson, CB – We should all celebrate Johnson’s 67-yard pick-six. Johnson, a target for criticism this season, made a fantastic play and helped lift the team when the offense was stuck. It wasn’t unlike the interception he had last year against the Cleveland Browns. It was a nice moment for a player who’s often looked like his best football is behind him. Devin Bush, LB – I was critical of Bush just a couple weeks ago, and correctly, told. I was wrong by you, the readers. And I appreciate that. I cannot deny though, that Bush was awesome against Tampa. He was flying around, making plays everywhere. He led the Bears with nine tackles, two passes defensed and a tackle for loss. Cameron Lewis, DB – Cam Lewis nabbed his first interception since 2024. He also finished with five tackles and a pass breakup. For a player who was seen more as a depth piece and back up, he’s played well. Stock down Caleb Williams, QB – This is not a long-term down. In fact, if it were a real stock market, I’d be buying the dip. But after four interceptions, he has to get knocked a little bit. Two of them were on throwaways that just didn’t make it to the sideline, one was a tipped pass. The other was just a case of trusting his arm a little too much and getting fooled by Tampa’s disguise. The main reason I’m not worried is that it’s a total outlier in his career. It was the first time he’s had more than two interceptions in a game. All of his other regular-season multi-interception games came as a rookie. In fact, they were the second and third games of his career. So for his first 3+ interception game to come in game No. 40, I feel like is an OK thing. D’Andre Swift, RB – The bye week is much needed for Swift. The running game has looked rough against two fo the best run defenses in the league. It’s gotten the job done at times, but it hasn’t looked the best. Swift has looked banged up. Hopefully a week off will get him rested and ready for the stretch run of the season. And getting his stablemate, Kyle Monangai, back will help too. Zavion Thomas, WR – The rookie nearly earned a spot in the stock up category this week. His kick return was brilliant, and called back through no fault of his own. The one pass he didn’t catch wasn’t the easiest catch to make, so I wasn’t going to hold it against him. But his penalty for unnecessary roughness after a play, back Chicago up and Caleb was intercepted on the next play. While I don’t think everything that happened afterward was a direct result, it certainly shifted momentum in the moment. He didn’t get another offensive snap after it. Players just can’t make those kinds of mistakes. Who is up and down in your eyes this week? Next week, I’ll look at who is up and down for the season so far. Let me know who ’ s caught your eye through the first nine games.

stories.title: Source: Ravens, now on third kicker, sign journeyman Riley Patterson
stories.summary: The Raven signed journeyman kicker Riley Patterson after his workout for the team on Wednesday, according to NFL Network.
stories.detailText: OWINGS MILLS, Md. -- In the Ravens ' most volatile season with kickers, Baltimore signed journeyman Riley Patterson after his workout for the team on Wednesday, a source told NFL Network's Mike Garafolo. Patterson, 27, was cut by the Miami Dolphins on Oct. 20 after going 7-of-9 on field goals this season and struggling on kickoffs. This marks the first time in the Ravens' 31-year history that they've used three kickers in a single season. Baltimore placed Tyler Loop (groin) on injured reserve on Nov. 3 and then had Jake Moody signed off its practice squad by the Atlanta Falcons on Tuesday. Moody hit a 53-yard field goal in a 33-10 loss to the Jacksonville Jaguars on Thursday, but he chose to go to Atlanta, where he has the opportunity to play his home games indoors. "Moody had a chance to be here," Ravens coach Jesse Minter said. "He had a choice to make and went somewhere else, [and I'll] leave it at that." Patterson earned a spot with Baltimore by beating out a group of free agent kickers, which included Harrison Mevis . The Ravens will need Patterson for at least three more games while Loop is on injured reserve. This is the 10th NFL team for Patterson, who has previously been with the Minnesota Vikings , New England Patriots , Detroit Lions , Jaguars, Cleveland Browns , Washington Commanders , New York Jets , Falcons, Dolphins and Ravens. In his six-year career, Patterson has made 97-of-112 field goals (86.6%), which ranks 12th among kickers with at least 50 attempts since 2021. He is 7-of-14 from 50 yards or longer. Patterson will kick for the Ravens on Monday night, when they host the winless Los Angeles Chargers .

stories.title: Longtime NFL QB and former NC State QB Philip Rivers reportedly set to be Wolfpack's new head coach
stories.summary: Rivers had been negotiating with NC State since at least Sunday.
stories.detailText: After multiple days of negotiations , Philip Rivers is set to become NC State's new head football coach. Per On3, the school will hire the former Wolfpack QB to take over at the end of the season. NC State fired Dave Doeren after a 3-4 start to the 2026 season that included a disastrous loss to Vanderbilt. Rivers, 44, doesn't have any collegiate coaching experience and is currently the head coach at St. Michael Catholic High School in Alabama. His son, Gunner Rivers, is St. Michael's QB. Gunner Rivers is a longtime NC State commit and a four-star prospect in the class of 2027. NC State is 4-5 after a loss to Duke in Week 10. The Wolfpack need to win two of their final three games under interim coach Todd Goebbel to make a bowl game. Doeren had been NC State's coach since 2013 and led the school to eight seasons of eight or more wins. The Wolfpack were 8-5 in 2025 but lost back-to-back games to Wake Forest and Stanford before Doeren was fired. In Week 3, QB CJ Bailey fumbled in the NC State end zone while trying to run out the clock to secure a victory. Vanderbilt recovered the ball and won 35-31. Rivers was a four-year QB at NC State from 2000 to 2003 before he was the No. 4 pick in the 2004 NFL Draft. He was drafted by the Giants and then traded to the Chargers, as Eli Manning didn't want to play for San Diego. Before he was drafted, Rivers was the 2003 ACC player of the year. He finished seventh in Heisman voting that season. Rivers played 16 seasons with the Chargers before playing his final full NFL season with the Indianapolis Colts in 2020. He was then out of the league for four seasons before the Colts signed him near the end of the 2025 season because of Daniel Jones' Achilles injury. Rivers started three games as the Colts attempted to make the playoffs, but Indianapolis lost all three and missed the postseason.

stories.title: As competitor, QB Daniel Jones wasn’t happy to see Colts as recent major trade sellers
stories.summary: Colts QB Daniel Jones voiced his recent displeasure over the team’s recent trades, but understood, it’s outside the players’ control.
stories.detailText: INDIANAPOLIS, INDIANA - NOVEMBER 08: Daniel Jones #17 of the Indianapolis Colts reacts against the Dallas Cowboys after the game at Lucas Oil Stadium on November 08, 2026 in Indianapolis, Indiana. (Photo by Michael Hickey/Getty Images) | Getty Images Indianapolis Colts starting quarterback Daniel Jones publicly voiced his disappointment that his struggling team was a recent major seller ahead of this past Tuesday’s league-wide trade deadline, while acknowledging, at least in his eyes, that it outside the players’ control ( via the Athletic’s James Boyd ): Daniel Jones, asked about the #Colts making trades for the future while he’s trying to win in the present: “You’re not happy to see a lot of those decisions, but like I said, that’s outside of our control. And our job is to play. Be prepared and play well. …” pic.twitter.com/0BH46dDY8x — James Boyd (@RomeovilleKid) November 11, 2026 In fairness, as a competitor, it would be a tough pill to swallow as a starting quarterback, knowing that your already below average wide receiver room to whom you regularly throw the football to is now without two of its best wideouts: Keenan Allen and Josh Downs—who were traded to San Francisco and Kansas City respectively. It looks like still rehabbing Colts top wideout Alec Pierce is not coming back to the football field anytime soon, and you also lost your perennial All-Pro left guard Quenton Nelson, who consistently helped keep you upright in pass protection, as he was traded to Seattle to help jumpstart the ongoing rebuild for Indianapolis. That being said, it’s not as though Jones and his teammates, including those who recently were traded, didn’t share in culpability to what led to the team’s recent fire sale. The team currently sits at 2-7, and among their defeats, lost to a winless Tennessee Titans team at home. Their brutal loss led to their longtime general manager Chris Ballard being fired thereafter, and that was the first domino to fall regarding the recent sell-off. Two weeks later, the Colts would go on to be blown out in Jacksonville, 42-7, and it was clear their season was definitively over—if it wasn’t already, after that dreadful rock bottom showing. The Colts have now lost 5 straight games in 2026. Dating back to 2025, they’ve lost 14 of their last 14 regular season games. In particular, after landing a 2-year, potential $100 million contract extension, Jones, who’s coming off a torn Achilles, has struggled this season and provided the Colts well below average starting quarterback play in 2026. He’s completed 182 of 302 pass attempts (60.3%) for 1,722 total passing yards, 6 passing touchdowns, and 10 interceptions during 9 starts so far in the 2026 campaign. It’s not all Jones’ fault offensively though. Even before the recent wide receiver trades, this was one of the league’s worst wide receiver rooms collectively without Pierce back. It now resembles closer to a 2nd-team preseason squad. His pass protection also hasn’t been great, even when Nelson was here, as a number of once reliable o-linemen have since struggled in pass protection. That being said, a starting quarterback is the league’s most valuable position, and almost always, if you don’t have a ‘dude’ there, who can consistently elevate his teammates, carry the offense for stretches, and make pivotal, even difficult winning plays late in games, the whole team will struggle—or at least reach its inevitable end.

stories.title: Colts rightfully noncommittal on whether WR Alec Pierce will still return this 2026 season
stories.summary: For those holding out hope for Alec Pierce returning this season, I wouldn’t count on it for the Colts.
stories.detailText: INDIANAPOLIS, IN - DECEMBER 28: Alec Pierce #14 of the Indianapolis Colts runs out of the tunnel prior to an NFL football game against the Jacksonville Jaguars at Lucas Oil Stadium on December 28, 2025 in Indianapolis, Indiana. (Photo by Cooper Neill/Getty Images) | Getty Images Indianapolis Colts head coach Shane Steichen was rightfully non-committal on whether rehabbing lead wideout Alec Pierce will still return this season—and rightfully so ( via The Athletic’s James Boyd ): #Colts HC Shane Steichen, asked if WR Alec Pierce (heel/IR) has a chance to return this season: “We’ll see. Like I said last week, he’s still in that rehab process, and I’m not going to put a timetable on return.” — James Boyd (@RomeovilleKid) November 11, 2026 The Colts returning lead wideout from last season has been out since Week 2 on the road against the Kansas City Chiefs, when he reinjured his left heel and was subsequently placed on injured reserve. Pierce had previously missed all of this past training camp and preseason after undergoing a once thought minor cleanup surgery on that same heel in late March. However, after an expedited return to the football field, he reinjured it just a few weeks later on Sunday Night Football primetime. He hasn’t played for the Colts since. On the 2026 season, Pierce has 5 receptions for 72 total receiving yards during 2 starts. Of course, with the Colts currently sitting at a disappointing 2-7, and having undergone a recent fire sale of key veterans and even some young players alike, it doesn’t make much sense to rush Pierce back to the football field again anytime soon—even though Indianapolis was initially targeting (and realistically hopeful) for a potential midseason return. It’s not like they certainly couldn’t use Pierce given their remaining patchwork wide receiver room of Laquon Treadwell, Ashton Dulin, Nick Westbrook-Ikhine, Anthony Gould, and rookie Deion Burks, but with this clearly being another lost season in Indianapolis, there’s no reason to risk him suffering another setback. Giving that we’re in Week 10, it seems as though the Colts have pushed back that potential midseason return, and if Pierce even does return much later in the season, it will likely mean that he’s fully, and I mean fully cleared physically. He shouldn’t be rushed or have his return to the football field expedited by any means whatsoever. My calculated safe guess though is that we won’t see him until the start of the 2027 campaign for the Colts.

LP = Limited participant in practice. DNP = Did not participate in practice. NIR = Not injury related. PUP = Physically unable to participate list. IR = Injured reserve. Note: only starters on IR are listed. Player Name* = Starter. Injury designation definitions: Probable = the league defines a Probable injury designation as a 75% or greater chance of playing. Historically, 95% of players designated probable are active and played on game day. Questionable = the league defines a Questionable injury designation as being ‘uncertain’ of whether the player will play or not. This replaces the former definition of having a 50% chance of playing. Historically, 70-75% of players with a Questionable injury designation were active and played on game day. Doubtful = The league defines a Doubtful injury designation to mean the player is unlikely to participate in the game. In practical terms, teams use the designation when a player has less than a 50% chance to suit up, and active game appearances from this designation remain rare. Historically only around 6% of players with a Doubtful designation are active and played on game day. Out = will not play. Players with this designation are not active on game day and league rules prohibit them from playing. Notes on Injured Players For the Vikings, Blake Cashman is the most significant player on the list as he is in concussion protocol. It is not typical for players to clear the concussion protocol and not miss at least one game, and this being a short week makes if probably even less likely. We’ll see how he progresses but it’s reasonable at this point to expect that Cashman will miss the Packers game. Cashman was the only player Kevin O’Connell pointed out in his press conference on Wednesday, meaning he was the one most at risk of not playing on Sunday, although Kyler Murray isn’t likely to be active for Sunday’s game either. Micah Parsons has had his 3-week window open to return from the PUP list, but I suspect the plan has always been for him to return after the Packers bye-week, which follows Sunday’s game. He was also suffering from an illness on Wednesday. But I don’t see that he’s been ramping up much yet where he would play on Sunday, although he is expected to participate in some 11-on-11 activities in practice this week. The Packers interior offensive line starters are all on the injury list. Aaron Banks has been on the injury list pretty much the whole season for the Packers and hasn’t played much, so difficult to tell whether he’ll play on Sunday or not. He has a new hip injury. Center Sean Rhyan being a DNP is notable and not a good sign for his availability on Sunday having missed the last two games with the same ankle injury. Kevin Zeitler’s ankle seems more like something he can play through at this point. He was just inserted into the starting offensive line last week after spending several weeks ramping up after being acquired. Defensively, outside of Parsons, Lukas Van Ness, Javon Bullard, and Zaire Franklin are players to watch. Both are starters that had DNP statuses on Wednesday. Franklin has missed the last three games so his not practicing isn’t a good sign for Sunday availability although Packers head coach Matt LaFleur expressed some optimism about him being able to practice later this week. He also didn’t completely close the door on Rhyan being available on Sunday. Van Ness’ injury is new, so unclear how severe it is at this point. Javon Bullard had to come out of the game a few times last week due to injury so unclear if his injuries will keep him out or not. Lastly, Packers kicker Trey Smack is dealing with a calf injury on his kicking leg, so another player to watch later this week. We’ll have updates tomorrow and Friday with injury designations. stories.title: What Reggie Gilliam’s return designation means for the Patriots
stories.summary: The Patriots fullback has been designated to return from injured reserve.
stories.detailText: For the first time in five weeks, the New England Patriots had a traditional fullback at practice on Wednesday. Reggie Gilliam, who was initially placed on injured reserve due to knee and ankle injuries in early October, made his comeback during his team’s final session before its trip to Germany for the upcoming Week 10 meeting with the Detroit Lions. This means he is now officially designated to return from IR. Let’s check out how this impacts the Patriots for the time being. Clock starts ticking We will get into the actual on-field impact of a potential Gilliam return to the 53-man roster once/if he is activated. For now, at least, the window for such a follow-up move has been opened. This means that, at least theoretically, Gilliam could be back on the game day roster as soon as this Sunday against the Lions. He will join the rest of the team on the flight to Germany, so there is an option New England could activate him in time for the game. They don’t have to, however: the team has 21 days to make that call before the return window will close again. If not activated at that point, Gilliam would revert back to injured reserve to end his season. Obviously, with return designations limited — more on that in a second — the expectation is is that the 29-year-old will eventually return to the 53-man roster when all is said and done. Two guys, one spot Following Monday’s release of tight end Tanner Arkin — a move that might hint at a potential Gilliam activation given that the rookie served as a stand-in fullback over the last few weeks — the Patriots have 52 of the 53 spots on their active roster occupied. This means that they could easily activate Gilliam without having to make a follow-up move. There is only one problem: he is not the only player currently in the 21-day window. Interior offensive lineman Greg Van Roten, who was the next man up after starting right guard Mike Onwenu fractured his ankle in September, returned to practice last week. He too is a candidate to be activated, especially given the current state of New England’s interior offensive line. Fact is, in order to bring both of them back, somebody will have to be removed from the active roster. There are several options, but one of them can effectively be ruled out: a player getting cut. With the Patriots taking their entire healthy roster to Germany, one of the 52 players getting handed his walking papers seems like a highly unlikely outcome. What is more likely is that only one of them will be brought back this week, or that the additional spot for a second activation will be created by moving another player to an injury list. There are multiple candidates such as the three non-participants during Wednesday’s practice — RB TreVeyon Henderson, OL Ben Brown, CB Carlton Davis — or offensive lineman Walter Rouse, who currently finds himself in concussion protocol. Another returnee The NFL allows every team to bring up to eight players back from injured reserve during the regular season. With Gilliam now getting designated as such a return player, the Patriots have used up five of those already. They previously designated wide receivers A.J. Brown and Mack Hollins as well as offensive linemen Marcus Bryan and the aforementioned Greg Van Roten for activation. All but Van Roten currently reside on the 53-man roster, with the O-lineman in the 21-day window alongside Gilliam. This also means that only three spots are left for the six eligible players currently remaining on injured reserve: WR Romeo Doubs, RG Mike Onwenu, LG Alijah Vera-Tucker, ED Quintayvious Hutchins, LB Khalil Jacobs, and S Dell Pettus. Doubs and Vera-Tucker appear to be the frontrunners to be brought back from that group both considering their injuries and importance to the roster as a whole. By the way, whether or not Gilliam (or Van Roten, for that matter) is actually activated to the 53-man roster is immaterial to the designation. He counts against those eight available return spots regardless.

stories.title: Cowboys report card: Grading the first half of the season
stories.summary: How would you grade the Cowboys at the halfway point?
stories.detailText: Photo by Lauren Leigh Bacho/Getty Images | Getty Images If the first nine weeks of the regular season were like an amusement park ride for the Dallas Cowboys, they’d be bumper cars. You remember them being great as a kid, so you’re excited to hop in the car and take it for another spin. It’s different. Now that you’re older, the mystique is gone. The gas pedal doesn’t work anymore; sometimes you don’t fit in the car, and you walk out with more back pain than you’ve felt in your lifetime. The defense is the cool bumper car in the corner no one can seem to fix, and the offense is the bumper car that can only turn right. After Brian Schottenheimer’s first year as head coach finished with a 7-9-1 record, it feels as if the team has somehow taken a step back. In the first four weeks of the season, it looked like the offense would carry the defense to the finish line. After three horrible losses to the Tampa Bay Buccaneers, Green Bay Packers, and Arizona Cardinals, the Cowboys’ offense struggled to find its identity. There have been some bright spots over nine weeks and a win over the Indianapolis Colts helps, but the report card for the first half of the season isn’t filled with A-grades, despite the roster’s star power. A grades: Quinnen Williams (A): When Quinnen Williams signed his contract extension with the Cowboys this offseason, it set the clock on whether or not the Micah Parsons trade officially pays off. It took Williams some time to find his footing in a system he hasn’t played in since college, but over the last five weeks he looks like an All-Pro at defensive tackle. Quinnen Williams in 2026 Weeks 1-4: • 13 tackles, 1 sack, 4 TFLs, 3 QB hits Weeks 5-9: • 23 tackles, 4 sacks, 10 TFLs, 6 QB hits Big Q has turned a big corner. #DallasCowboys pic.twitter.com/kBdkJEvMNA — Brandon Loree (@Brandoniswrite) November 9, 2026 Among all defensive tackles, Williams is tied for fifth in sacks (5), third in total pressures (31), and is first in tackles for loss (14). His leadership in the locker room has been praised as a big reason why the defense is starting to turn a corner. Just like his counterpart on offense, Dak Prescott, Williams will have to help carry his unit the rest of the way if they want to make a postseason push, starting Sunday vs. the 49ers. CeeDee Lamb (A): After starting out of the gate extremely hot, CeeDee Lamb cooled off vs. the Packers, Cardinals, and Bucs. He had a dominant performance against the Philadelphia Eagles, but against those three teams, Lamb caught 18 passes for 137 yards and zero touchdowns. Then he bounced back vs. the Colts, with 10 receptions for 195 yards and a touchdown in the absence of George Pickens. The offense needs to be more consistent with getting Lamb the ball because when he is cooking defensive backs, this team looks better overall. In four out of the five games where Lamb has scored a touchdown, Dallas has won. It’s not always that simple, but in this case, it might be. His ability to bring up the entire team keeps him at an A grade for the year. Tyler Guyton (A-): No one has surprised more this season than Tyler Guyton and his development. The Cowboys have put all their faith in Guyton and never gave up on him, and it’s paid off. Guyton might not be a Pro Bowl player yet, but he’s looked better than he has in the last two years at left tackle and, more importantly, has stayed healthy. Coming into the year, he was the team’s biggest question mark. Now he’s turned into one of the team’s most consistent players up front. Joey Porter Jr. (A-): Like Lamb, Joey Porter Jr. has been able to raise all boats when he’s been healthy and on the field. I think it's safe to say that Joey Porter Jr. has quickly become one of the most valuable players for the #Cowboys . https://t.co/JHIts03BvE pic.twitter.com/783t3Tb0a2 — John Owning (@JohnOwning) November 3, 2026 The biggest disappointment of Porter’s tenure so far in Dallas is that he hasn’t been fully healthy and has been bouncing between the field and the sideline. That’s why this grade is more on a curve of what he can be. He rolled his ankle in practice a few weeks ago, and he doesn’t seem 100 percent healthy, considering he only played 36 snaps on defense vs. the Cardinals and missed the Colts game. Christian Parker has shown he likes to rotate his cornerbacks, but JPJ needs to be on the field for almost every snap when healthy because of his impact. The Cowboys don’t have their bye week until Week 14, so they may have to manage him until then, but he’s been an All-Pro-level corner when he locks down wide receivers for Dallas. B grades: Dak Prescott (B+): There have certainly been A+ moments for the Cowboys quarterback, but overall, Dak Prescott has been very good this season—not elite. His inability to find answers against the blitz, which he’s normally great at, hurts him here. Prescott was phenomenal in the second half of the Houston Texans game and in the Philadelphia Eagles matchup, but given what those teams have turned into, it wasn’t high-level competition. Prescott is currently third among quarterbacks in passing yards (2,381), tied for seventh in touchdown passes (16), and is third in quarterback rating (77.0). The second half of the season will define his 2026 campaign more as he tries to dig Dallas out of the playoff hole they’re in right now. He’ll have to do it against big-time competition in the San Francisco 49ers, Jacksonville Jaguars, and Seattle Seahawks. Otito Ogbonnia (B): Just when the pro personnel department looks like its decision-making needs to be questioned, they find a diamond in the rough like Otito Ogbonnia. The Cowboys defensive tackle has been a force in stopping the run. Ogbonnia leads all defensive linemen with 18 run stops, per Pro Football Focus. Prior to joining Dallas, Ogbonnia never had more than 12 stops in a season. He’s only here on a one-year deal, but the Cowboys need to find a way to re-sign him to a long-term contract because he’s shown he’s worthy of it, and he complements what Dallas wants to do up front with their defensive tackle rotation. Javonte Williams (B): The Cowboys bell cow picked up right where he left off a season ago. After having a career year in Dallas, Javonte Williams looks poised to repeat the same success that earned him a contract extension this offseason. Williams sits ninth in rushing yards for the year (629), averaging 4.1 yards per carry, and is tied for second in rushing touchdowns (9). While the Cowboys were trying to find their identity in the run game, there were a few times Williams didn’t seem to see the holes well or couldn’t bounce the ball outside. He’s never going to be Bijan Robinson or Jahmyr Gibbs, but he can be the best back Dallas needs when they are trying to establish the run. Look no further than his career performance vs. the Eagles when he rushed for 155 yards off 25 carries. Caleb Downs faced his older brother Josh for the first time in the NFL and delivered his best performance yet. 3 TKL, 1 SACK, 1 INT, 2 PD, 1 TFL vs Colts. The rookie was making plays everywhere and is looking like a future star for Dallas. pic.twitter.com/DhpDtwsSdl — Football Performances (@NFLPerformances) November 8, 2026 C grades: Cowboys Top 3 rookies (C+): Caleb Downs’ and Jaishawn Barham’s performance vs. the Baltimore Ravens is doing the heavy lifting for the overall grade of Dallas’ top three draft picks. Downs has had to rotate from nickel corner to safety a few times this season while the defense dealt with injuries in the secondary. That’s a lot for a rookie—even one with his football intelligence—to process. That’s why at times Downs has looked like a fish out of water. However, his game vs. the Colts is exactly what the Cowboys hoped for when drafting him and what they’re hoping to see the rest of the season. As for Barham and first-round pick Malachi Lawrence, there have been moments, but largely inconsistent. With DeMarvion Overshown coming back healthy, Barham is back on the bench, where it might be better for him to take some time and learn more from his peers. As a downhill defender in the run game, Barham has shown to have high-level instincts and a feel for finding the ball carrier. But in the passing game, he’s looked lost and slow, which makes him a liability on third down. Lawrence may be done for the season, going on injured reserve after the Arizona Cardinals game. The hope is that he will return for the year, but depending on what the next three weeks look like, Dallas may decide to shut him down for 2026 and look toward 2027. This year was all about getting the reps at the NFL level, so it’s disappointing to see him put on the shelf for critical moments in his development. Prior to the injury, Lawrence was starting to stack some good weeks. Terence Steele (C+): The Cowboys’ right tackle has been very average so far, which is actually a win considering what we’ve seen in the past. Terence Steele hasn’t been Lane Johnson, but he also hasn’t been Chaz Green this year. His pass blocking has improved, allowing only three sacks, which is near a career low for him . Before his knee injury, Steele was known to be a mauler in the run game. That hasn’t shown up as much this year, considering Dallas’ run success has come when they go behind Tyler Guyton and Tyler Smith. If Steele can stay at a C+ grade for the rest of the season, then there shouldn’t be any reason why Prescott isn’t finding his receivers and going through his progressions. I’m sure most coaches around the league would take average play from their tackles as long as they don’t get beat. George Pickens (C): The curious case of George Pickens. Was he ever going to repeat the All-Pro version of himself we saw in 2025? Probably not with a healthy CeeDee Lamb in the lineup. But up to this point, Pickens has disappointed given the expectations before the season. To tell you the truth, it’s not his fault either. Yes, he could be a better blocker in the run game, but there shouldn’t be a game where Brevyn Spann-Ford has more targets in the passing attack than Pickens. Brian Schottenheimer has to do a better job of manufacturing touches for Pickens. Similar to his counterpart in Lamb, when Pickens gets rolling, he’s virtually unstoppable. Just look at what Ja’Marr Chase and Tee Higgins are doing in Cincinnati with the Bengals. Cowboys fans can only hope the second half of the season looks more like that for the duo in Dallas. Kenny Clark (C-): With the arrival of Quinnen Williams last year, a lot of the pressure came off Kenny Clark to be “that dude” on the interior of the D-line. Having him and Williams together as a tandem was set up to be the best defensive tackle duo Dallas has ever had. Like many players in this grade range, there have been moments when it looks like Clark can turn back the clock to his old self, but he also looks like a player past his prime who can’t consistently play the way he’s supposed to. At 31, Clark is on track to have the lowest PFF grade of his career: 57.4. He’s been generating pressures and is above league average with 20 among starting defensive tackles, but it’s not good enough given the expectations around him coming into the year. He’s a great leader in the locker room and will be great for a player like LT Overton, but for now, Clark has been okay through the first half of the season. D grades: All of the Cowboys’ outside linebackers (D): Taking Malachi Lawrence out of the mix, the most disappointing thing about the Cowboys this season has been their inability to get sacks or production from their outside linebackers. Donovan Ezeiruaku, Rashan Gary, and Von Miller have provided no juice when rushing the quarterback. Most of their sacks this year, which isn’t many to begin with, have come when Williams pressures the middle or when they get coverage sacks. Ezeiruaku was supposed to take a huge step forward in year two and get close to the pass-rushing production he had at Boston College. Only 2.5 sacks at this point in the year is not what the Cowboys were hoping for. Miller was supposed to roll out of bed and get eight sacks. He’s only recorded one sack through nine games. Then there’s Rashan Gary. He is on the leadership council and is consistently showing up on the Cowboys Sounds from the Sidelines , hyping up defenders around him, which is great. The running game has been a disaster, and he hasn’t been able to set the edge. He might not be the same pass rusher he once was, but when Gary arrived in Dallas, the expectation was that he could replace what the defense was missing when DeMarcus Lawrence left. If it wasn’t for Malachi Lawrence’s injury, the coaching staff would have to think hard about making Gary a rotation player and giving the rookie more snaps. Unfortunately, Dallas needs Gary to be a starter, considering there’s no one else, and Miller is a liability in the running game too. With BT Jordan in the building as a pass-rush specialist, the hope was that he could get these guys to perform at a high level, as he has with the Broncos in Denver. With seven of Dallas’ 17 total sacks this year coming from their outside linebackers, it’s not the coaching that’s poor; it might be a lack of talent at the position.

stories.title: Winners and losers from Ravens’ Week 9 loss to the Jaguars
stories.summary: Too many of the Ravens’ highly-paid veterans are dragging down the team during their four-game losing streak.
stories.detailText: BALTIMORE, MD - NOVEMBER 05: Marlon Humphrey #44 of the Baltimore Ravens looks on from the field during an NFL football game against the Jacksonville Jaguars at M&T Bank Stadium on November 5, 2026 in Baltimore, Maryland. (Photo by Cooper Neill/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Baltimore Ravens’ 33-10 loss to the Jacksonville Jaguars was their third consecutive game decided by at least 22 points. There was more bad than good in this one for the Ravens, as you would expect in such a lopsided contest. Winners RB Justice Hill: Hill was one of the few bright spots for Baltimore on Thursday night. The seventh-year veteran showed he still had burst on a 65-yard touchdown run in the fourth quarter. Hill’s 85 rushing yards were the most allowed to a single player by the Jaguars in their last 24 games. C Cam Jurgens: Jurgens rebounded from a poor game last week with a solid outing against Jacksonville. His 72.7 PFF grade was the highest of any offensive player for the Ravens. RG Vega Ioane: Ioane’s return to the lineup after missing the previous game with a knee injury was a welcome sight. The rookie’s 66.7 PFF grade was only behind Jurgens among offensive players. RT Roger Rosengarten: Rosengarten allowed zero pressures against the Jaguars and was third among offensive players with a 66.4 PFF grade. Losers QB Joe Fagnano: The rookie undrafted quarterback making his first start on a short week with an injured ankle played how you would expect. Fagnano struggled to move the ball through the air, racking up just 60 yards on 18 attempts, while throwing two interceptions. LG John Simpson: Simpson has been perhaps the most criticized starter on Baltimore’s offensive line after signing a three-year, $30 million contract this offseason. His 4.5 pass-blocking grade against Jacksonville should only stoke the flames. TE Mark Andrews: Highly-paid veterans continue to let the Ravens down this season, and no player exemplifies that more than their once Pro Bowl tight end. Andrews and Ronnie Stanley appear to be in competition at this point for who can have the most false starts, as the duo committed the penalty on consecutive plays to move the ball back 10 yards on second down. Andrews later fumbled the handoff on a fourth down, turning the ball over on downs. CB Marlon Humphrey: Humphrey continues to draw the ire of fans with comments made off the field, and his play on it only strengthens the criticism. Humphrey allowed a 52-yard completion to a tight end on the game’s opening drive when he appeared to get stuck watching Trevor Lawrence on a scramble, allowing the rookie Nate Boerkircher to get behind him down the field. WR LaJohntay Wester: Wester has failed to make much of an impact in the return game this season, and his lost fumble on a kickoff against the Jaguars could put his job security in question.

stories.title: Duke Tobin sends out 'not comfortable' head coach Zac Taylor to explain Bengals' trade-deadline snafu with Eagles
stories.summary: Zac Taylor almost certainly had little to nothing to do with the trade-deadline snafu in which the Bengals backed out of an agreed-upon deal with the Eagles. But he was left to explain it.
stories.detailText: Zac Taylor almost certainly had little to nothing to do with the trade-deadline snafu on Tuesday in which the Cincinnati Bengals backed out of an agreed-upon deal with the Philadelphia Eagles. But he was left to explain it. On Wednesday, the Bengals’ head coach took the podium to discuss the topic despite declaring that he was "not comfortable" doing so. He said he did it at the behest of director of player personnel and de facto general manager Duke Tobin. Per Taylor, Tobin is "really apologetic." To be clear, that came from Taylor's mouth, not Tobin's. Taylor: 'I'm not comfortable' "Obviously, we tried something yesterday," Taylor said. "Duke was very explicit with me when he came and spoke to me of how he wanted this portrayed. I'm not comfortable doing it, but I'm going to do what he asked. "We did make an effort to kind of put some depth in there in place of Cashius [Howell]. As we got into it, obviously it was going to be a little more costly than we initially anticipated. He's really apologetic about it and wants to make clear: Philly was a great trade partner. It was on our end." #Bengals HC Zac Taylor, speaking for GM Duke Tobin, says he’s very apologetic about how the Arnold Ebiketie trade fell apart. “Philly was a great trade partner. It was on our end.” pic.twitter.com/kHjzf7UWE6 — Ari Meirov (@MySportsUpdate) November 11, 2026 Embarrassing oversight by Bengals front office In case you missed it, the Bengals had an agreement with the Eagles in place to acquire edge rusher Arnold Ebiketie prior to Tuesday's trade deadline. The Bengals need depth at the position due to a wrist injury that placed Howell on injured reserve. In the agreed upon deal, the Bengals would’ve sent a sixth-round pick to the Eagles and received Ebiketie in return. But it turns out the deal came at a significantly higher cost, which the Bengals’ front office apparently didn't realize when it made the agreement. Per the NFL's compensatory picks mechanisms, the Bengals would’ve also had to forfeit a third-round compensatory pick to acquire Ebiketie. So in essence, they would have parted with a third-round pick and a sixth-round pick to acquire a backup pass rusher. Bengals appeared to realize their mistake via social media post It's a price that's prohibitive and one the Bengals reportedly didn't realize until Over the Cap's self-proclaimed "Compensatory Picks Guy™" Nick Korte pointed it out on social media . Arnold Ebiketie was signed as a compensatory free agent by the Eagles. The Bengals lost 3 CFAs and signed 2 (Cordell Volson not qualifying), thus while they gain a 2027 6th rounder, they lose a 2027 3rd round comp pick that was via Trey Hendrickson going to Baltimore. https://t.co/DxWAA8L0KN — Nick Korte (@nickkorte) November 10, 2026 Korte's analysis picked up traction among traditional NFL media, and only then did the Bengals back out of the deal , having realized its true cost. This was all reported Tuesday, and Taylor was left to confirm it with media on Wednesday. Why was Taylor left to answer for this? This is not Taylor's job. He's a head football coach. He's not supposed to be tasked with knowing the complex mechanics of NFL trades or the league's compensatory pick system, and he's not the one who pulled the trigger on the agreement with the Eagles. Those responsibilities lie with the player personnel arm of Cincinnati's front office, which is run by Tobin. The mistake was an embarrassment for Tobin's department that played out across sports media on Tuesday. On Wednesday, Tobin sent out Taylor to face the music.

teamStories.summary: No. 1 pick Fernando Mendoza said Wednesday it's a "once-in-a-lifetime" opportunity to be the Raiders' starting quarterback, while his teammates and coach expressed their confidence in his ability to lead the offense.
teamStories.detailText: HENDERSON, Nev. -- Thrust back into the spotlight after months as Kirk Cousins ' understudy, No. 1 pick Fernando Mendoza said Wednesday it's a "once-in-a-lifetime" opportunity to be the Las Vegas Raiders ' starting quarterback. Being the starter is a "new step" in his career, Mendoza said. Nonetheless, he's trying to avoid making the moment bigger than it has to be. Mendoza's starting debut Sunday will come against the reigning Super Bowl champions and one of the league's most imposing defenses, the Seattle Seahawks . Through his preparation and Cousins' mentorship since the spring, Mendoza is confident in his ability to run the offense and has gained the utmost trust from his teammates and coach Klint Kubiak. "I'm a lot more confident as a quarterback and feel more developed, whether it's [playing] under center, connecting with teammates, understanding an NFL scheme," Mendoza said Wednesday. "There are so many areas that I have improved on, and I look forward to keep on improving." Kubiak said this week shouldn't feel like a whirlwind for Mendoza because he has been preparing the right way from the beginning. Kubiak also said the Raiders will not be "peeling back anything" in their offense, as the coach is comfortable with Mendoza running the entire playbook. "We're going to go do what the whole team does best, all 11, and then he does his part distributing the football," Kubiak said. Mendoza's teammates understand the challenges of adjusting to the pro level and are rallying behind the 23-year-old signal-caller. Tight end Brock Bowers said he's "excited" for Mendoza's first start and can't wait to see him sling the ball around the field. Bowers said Mendoza has a good challenge ahead of him, facing a Seattle defense that has given up the fewest total yards per game in the league (244.2) and is tied for fourth in points allowed per game (18). "Everyone has faith in him," Bowers said. "[Mendoza] might have a bad play here and there, but you just got to flush it. I know he does a good job at that." Wide receiver Tre Tucker said there isn't anything Mendoza can't do and that he brings consistency, a trait Tucker likes to see from a quarterback. Tucker said Wednesday's practice with Mendoza as QB1 went "great" and it was good to see Mendoza in a flow. "We've been seeing it all year," Tucker said. "He's been taking reps with us. He's been doing everything, and you just see a throw in practice and say, 'Wow.' For that to be out there this Sunday is going to be fun." Despite all the attention on Mendoza, Cousins' absence in the locker room has been clearly felt. The Raiders' decision to trade Cousins to the Minnesota Vikings left many surprised, including Mendoza, who was in the locker room when the news broke. Mendoza said he had "no inkling" his mentor would be traded. "People were like, 'Kirk got traded,' and everyone just said that's the nature of the business, and that's how it is," Mendoza said. "And I'm excited to see Kirk in his future." Mendoza commended Cousins and his family for welcoming him with open arms. Cousins welcomed Mendoza into his household while in Las Vegas, was never dismissive and offered guidance without any conditions. "Everyone [saw] the Netflix show and you hear things from media, but to actually be in with him and spend long hours just in the quarterback room with him was extremely special," Mendoza said. "I'm going to miss him, and I really appreciate and am deeply thankful for everything that the Cousins family has offered to me." Starting center Tyler Linderbaum said he was "absolutely" surprised by Cousins' departure. He said Cousins put himself in a position where teams wanted him, but Linderbaum wished that hadn't been the case. Tucker said it was hard to see Cousins leave, calling him "one of the best human beings" he has ever met. But Tucker also said he knew the day was coming, which made it easier for him to handle the past 24 hours. Tucker said Cousins left the Raiders in a better place than he found them. One of Tucker's best memories was seeing the dynamic between Cousins and Mendoza. "How Kirk is now, that's how Fernando will be when he's Kirk's age," Tucker said. "They were great together."

teamStories.detailText: The Seattle Seahawks emerged victorious in an injury bowl against the Arizona Cardinals last week, and it appears they may have to do it again on Sunday against the Las Vegas Raiders. Seattle released the first of the three weekly injury reports, which is headlined by the health of backup quarterback Drew Lock, who is battling a lingering elbow injury and a new oblique injury. Lock was limited in practice on Wednesday, with head coach Mike Macdonald indicating that the veteran is “making good progress” and may start against the Raiders. The ominous messaging leaves the entirety of Seattle on Jalen Milroe watch yet again as the second-year player is the only other healthy quarterback on the Seahawks’ 53-man roster and would come in if Lock couldn’t play. Whoever is under center will once again be working with a patchwork offensive line as stars Quenton Nelson and Charles Cross did not practice. Nelson is battling a knee injury that might hold him out for his second straight game while Cross has been out with an ankle injury since Week 7. Backup guard Anthony Bradford continues to be hampered by a knee injury and was limited on Wednesday. The Seahawks offense appears to have a weapon returning as wide receiver and kicker returner Rashid Shaheed was a full participant in practice. Shaheed has had a quiet 2026, but remains a key piece to unlocking the Seahawks’ offense as the organization is hopeful he emerges as a second option beside Jaxon Smith-Njigba. On the defensive side, Leonard Williams remains out with a stinger that he suffered against the Kansas City Chiefs, and edge rusher Derick Hall was limited with a new back injury. Both would be a massive loss for the Seahawks front that will hope to ruin Raiders’ rookie Fernando Mendoza’s debut. It wasn’t all negative for the Seahawks’ defense, though, as signs are trending positive for edge rusher Uchenna Nwosu, who was limited with the ankle injury that’s held him out of the team’s last two games. Meanwhile, the Raiders report was considerably smaller, so it appears they’ll be near full-go against their former AFC West rival. For the Seahawks, they will have two more days of practice before setting game designations, so here’s to hoping that the report shrinks throughout the week. teamStories.summary: Kirk Cousins offered some thoughts on his trade to Minnesota after the news broke in the most on-brand location imaginable.
teamStories.detailText: Before Kirk Cousins could head to the Land of 10,000 Lakes after being traded to the Minnesota Vikings , he had to make an on-brand stop: at Great Clips. Cousins is a longtime aficionado of the budget-friendly salon chain, having been awarded its first-ever VIP card back in 2025 -- the "Hall of Fade" card affords free hair cuts to both Cousins and everyone who's at the location with him when it's used. But it wasn't just a haircut for Cousins on Tuesday. When the veteran quarterback dropped by Great Clips following the trade, they took the time to get his thoughts on the news. Reflecting on the trade, Cousins acknowledged that there was something in particular about the destination -- he quarterbacked the Vikings from 2018 to 2023 -- that made the transaction particularly special. "There's so many memories, so many great people," Cousins said. "I understand the challenge on the football field, there's a lot of work to go get done, but it would be really special. If you're going to go win somewhere and have success, I want it to be in Minnesota." He also had a message to Raiders supporters, complimenting the fanbase and organization for their hospitality in his short stay in Las Vegas. "To the fans in Vegas, I just feel so grateful for how they welcomed me with open arms for the several months I was here -- that includes teammates, the organization," he said. "I really couldn't speak more highly of my time here in Vegas." Cousins also addressed fans in Minnesota, saying he was excited to reunite with his former team -- though the roster wouldn't quite be the same as the one he left. "To the fans in Minnesota, I'm thrilled to have the chance to come back," he said. "And to hopefully write the ending to a story for me that started eight, nine years ago when I first arrived. Ready to take on this new challenge with this, really, new team in Minnesota and see where we can go." Asked for his parting thoughts before he left the hot seat (barber chair?), Cousins reflected on the balance between saying goodbye to his former team and also getting to reunite with a place he already had to depart. "I've got a lot of emotions right now that are mixed. Always difficult to say goodbye, especially to people that mean a great deal to me, and there are so many of them here in Vegas," he said. "There's also a lot of people waiting for me in Minnesota that mean a great deal to me, that it was difficult to say goodbye to three years ago."

Raiders QB Fernando Mendoza effusively thanks Kirk Cousins ahead of first NFL start
teamStories.summary: The Raiders' new starting quarterback has plenty of appreciation for the previous one.
teamStories.detailText: Fernando Mendoza's NFL career is set to begin in earnest on Sunday, with his first game as the starting quarterback of the Las Vegas Raiders . He credited one man in particular for helping him get there. Speaking to reporters Wednesday ahead of the Raiders' game against the Seattle Seahawks, Mendoza effusively thanked Las Vegas' previous starter, Kirk Cousins, for his mentorship over the past several months. Cousins was traded to the Minnesota Vikings on Tuesday , opening the door for Mendoza to start. The 23-year-old Mendoza said Cousins and his family were nothing but welcoming to him: "I wanted to make a statement where I really, truly, from the bottom of my heart, wanted to thank Kirk and the entire Cousins family, whether it was Julie, Cooper or Turner. They've, as a family, done so much for me. They've essentially taken me into their household when they were here, and they welcomed me with open arms. "It would have been really easy for Kirk to be the veteran quarterback, having already proved everything, to be more dismissive, but he had me with open arms and has taught me so many things. Whether it's film study, how to operate as a starting quarterback, all the different, multi-faceted approaches that have made him so successful throughout his career. He has shared with no restrictions or no constraints, so I really appreciate him." The Raiders signed Cousins to what was essentially a one-year, $20 million contract last offseason , in advance of selecting Mendoza with the first overall pick of the 2026 NFL Draft. The plan was clear: The 38-year-old Cousins was brought in to start under center for the beginning of the season while helping mold Mendoza into a franchise quarterback. Mendoza expressed his appreciation for all the help he received preparing under quarterbacks coach Mike Sullivan and backup quarterback Aidan O'Connell, but he acknowledged that there's ultimately no substitute for real playing time: "Those mental reps on the sidelines during games, they were crucial. Coach Sullivan and Aiden, they were great. However, there's nothing like game experience and game reps because the best vision is when you're in the pocket rather than adjacent on the sideline, just to process information." Mendoza did pump the brakes a bit when asked what "lasting memory" he would retain of Cousins as a teammate, noting with a laugh that the man was traded, not dead. "Well, I mean, he's not gone. Like, he's gone from the Raiders forever. He's not gone forever." Raiders vs. Seahawks and a new era of Las Vegas football kick off at 4:05 p.m. ET Sunday.

teamStories.title: Treydan Stukes provides silver lining in Las Vegas Raiders’ Week 9 blowout loss to San Francisco 49ers
teamStories.summary: The rookie safety was one of the few bright spots on defense this past Sunday.
teamStories.detailText: (Photo by Ezra Shaw/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Las Vegas Raiders’ defense is searching for answers after giving up 30 or more points for the sixth consecutive game in the Week 9 loss to the San Francisco 49ers . However, the Raiders might have found at least one solution with rookie safety Treydan Stukes. Stukes has been playing well and getting better just about every week, and last Sunday in San Francisco was his best performance to date. The former Arizona Wildcat nabbed his second career interception (first since the season opener) and yielded just 19 yards on five targets (four catches) while coming up with a couple of ‘ defensive stops ’ in coverage, according to Pro Football Focus . That was good enough to earn PFF’s fifth-highest coverage grade (85.8) among safeties for the week. While there’s plenty to be negative about when it comes to the Raiders’ defense, let’s focus on one of the few positives and break down the second-round pick’s outing. Treydan Stukes setting the edge against Trent Williams #Raiders pic.twitter.com/VeXMnHEK2k — Matt Holder (@MHolder95) November 10, 2026 As the numbers above indicate, Stukes’ impact was primarily in coverage against the 49ers. But the clip against the run above caught my eye. San Francisco comes out in 22 personnel with fullback Kyle Juszczyk as one of three strong-side tight ends initially. That’s how Kyle Shanahan likes to run 13 personnel plays/formations while keeping Juszczyk on the field. Meanwhile, the Raiders had the rookie safety cover George Kittle frequently throughout the game, so he’s on the line of scrimmage and on the strong side of the formation. When Juszczyk motions to the weak-side pre-snap, linebacker Quay Walker signals for Stukes to stay inside so that Stukes can cover Kittle with inside leverage if it’s a pass play. The problem with that is it puts a defensive back in the C-gap, where he’s in future Hall of Fame left tackle Trent Williams’ path if the 49ers run outside zone, which is exactly what Shanahan dials up. That’s a mismatch in the offense’s favor since a safety is taking on a block from one of (if not the) best offensive tackles in the game. However, the rookie doesn’t back down. Stukes eyes Kittle initially, and once he reads run, he redirects to take on Williams’ block and ends up resetting the line of scrimmage by winning at the point of attack. That helps force running back Christian McCaffrey to cut upfield and right into linebacker Tommy Eichenberg for a short gain. While Stukes doesn’t make the tackle here, he makes the play by beating a high-quality opponent in a disadvantageous matchup to force the running back to redirect into an unblocked defender. That’s pretty impressive run support from a defensive back. Nice close from Treydan Stukes -Spins down from 2-high to play curl/flat in C3 -Stays deep in his area to encourage short throw on 2nd & 20 -Rallies & tackles to put SF in 3 & 15 #RaiderNation pic.twitter.com/ep0mXrqzRv — Matt Holder (@MHolder95) November 10, 2026 But again, the safety’s impact was felt the most in the passing game. While the interception was undoubtedly the best play he made on the afternoon (don’t worry, that play is coming later), Stukes made a handful of quality tackles that kept San Francisco behind the sticks. Here, it’s second and 20, and the Raiders line up in a two-high look pre-snap before rolling a safety down into the curl-to-flat area and running Cover 3 post-snap. Stukes is the safety spinning into the second level, and he shows some situational awareness by staying deep in his area. That does two things: it makes it more difficult to throw a pass over his head and influences the quarterback to make a short throw. Thus, Brock Purdy throws the quick out route to the slot receiver, which is what the Raiders want him to do in this situation. That’s where Stukes’ closing speed comes in, as he rallies to the football and makes a nice open-field tackle to limit the yards after the catch. Now, San Francisco faces 3rd and 15. Just don’t ask what happens on the next play…(Purdy scrambles for 18 yards). Another quality coverage stop from Treydan Stukes -Eyes Kittle initially while dropping into C2 -Sees Kittle chip release into the flat -Shifts eyes to backfield & sees crossing route -Breaks on throw to make stop on 3rd & 5 #Raiders pic.twitter.com/ckJkQSdWmy — Matt Holder (@MHolder95) November 10, 2026 This time, Las Vegas starts in a one-high look and rotates into Cover 2. Stukes, playing nickelback, lines up over Kittle and is responsible for the hook-to-curl area of the coverage. Initially, the safety reads the tight end and sees the tight end chip block before releasing into a flat route, taking Kittle out of Stukes’ area/assignment. So, the rookie shifts his eyes to the backfield and starts looking for a crossing route from the other side of the field. Meanwhile, the 49ers have their outside receiver in the trips formation at the bottom of the screen run a drag route into Stukes’ area. He sees that, parks himself at the sticks and pounces once Purdy lets the ball go. That’s where the closing speed comes in, again, as he makes the tackle just short of the sticks to put the offense in a fourth-and-short situation. That set up one of the Raiders’ few stops last Sunday. 49ers do get 5 on 1st & 10 here, but this is a pretty impressive close from Treydan Stukes, covering a lot of ground to bring George Kittle down on the flat route #Raiders pic.twitter.com/SICgyiWlYi — Matt Holder (@MHolder95) November 10, 2026 Technically, this play is still a positive result for the offense since San Francisco gets five yards on first and 10 to stay on schedule. But considering the rookie safety’s assignment, this is still an impressive rep. He lines up as a deep safety in a two-high look pre-snap but is in man coverage with the tight end, Kittle. Meanwhile, the 49ers run an RPO where Kittle is on a flat route against not just off coverage, but a safety playing over 10 yards off the ball. That makes Purdy’s decision easy, as he aborts the run play and just dumps the ball into the flat. In theory, the tight end should have enough room to pick up the first down or at least set up the offense in a second-and-short situation. However, Stukes’ closing speed allows him to make contact right at the line of scrimmage despite how deep he was playing. Now, the tackle can be better since he does allow too many yards after contact. But Kittle is one of the hardest tight ends in the NFL to bring down, so there’s no shame in that. Plus, the defense still has a decent chance to get off the field in a second-and-five situation. Elite play from Treydan Stukes to get an INT -Starts in 2-high, rolls down for Curl-Flat in C3 -Picks up slot WR while keeping eyes on QB -Reads Purdy's eyes, comes off man/assignment & climbs ladder to make the pick #RaiderNation pic.twitter.com/HW1fzEUibA — Matt Holder (@MHolder95) November 9, 2026 Now, the moment you all have been waiting for: the aforementioned interception! What really makes this rep impressive is that the first-year pro makes a play where he shows the awareness or football IQ of a well-tenured veteran. As we’ve seen on a handful of occasions already, Stukes starts in two-high and spins down into a Cover 3 look. Granted, the play call is a little different, where Taron Johnson blitzes off the edge for a three-deep, three-under fire zone. That means the safety essentially takes over the nickel’s coverage assignment by picking up the slot receiver, who is running a return route (out and then in). Stukes’ eyes are the big key here. He’s staring in the backfield throughout the rep, using his peripheral vision to read the receiver’s route and match the receiver’s movement patterns step for step. So when Purdy rears back to throw, the rookie safety is able to read the quarterback’s eyes, come off his man and sink on the drag route from the other side of the field to climb the ladder and pick the pass off. This is what happens when instincts meet athleticism, as that was one hell of a catch too. Well done, rook, well done!
